## docs/schema/types.md

33 findings — 1 blocker, 8 major, 21 minor, 3 nit.

### [blocker] `matches`'s declared signature is the reverse of every call site, and the prose that explains it is incoherent with the calls

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:452, docs/schema/types.md:449, docs/auth.md:238, docs/schema/README.md:188, docs/schema/functions.md:103, docs/schema/queries.md:339, docs/schema/railroad.md:556
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#comparison
- **Evidence:** types.md:452 `matches : Hashed a -> a -> Bool` hashes its right-hand argument under the stored policy and compares in constant time.` Call sites, all of them: types.md:449 / functions.md:103 / railroad.md:556 ``attempt `matches` user.password``; README.md:188 ``attempt `matches` credential.secret``; queries.md:339 ``attempt `matches` u.password``; auth.md:232 ``attempt `matches` c.secret``. railroad.md:551-553: "Any named function may be written infix by enclosing it in backticks, as in Haskell, with Haskell's default fixity."
- **Why it is wrong:** Haskell backtick infix means ``x `f` y == f x y``, so ``attempt `matches` user.password`` elaborates to `matches attempt user.password`, requiring `attempt :: Hashed a` (the plaintext typed as the stored digest) and `user.password :: a` (the digest typed as plaintext). Under the declared signature the only well-typed spelling is ``user.password `matches` attempt``, which appears nowhere. auth.md:238 makes it worse in prose: "`matches` hashes its right-hand argument under the policy recorded on the stored value" — in every written call the right-hand argument *is* the stored value, so the sentence asks the runtime to hash the digest. This is the single mechanism for verifying every credential in the system.
- **Fix:** In docs/schema/types.md#comparison, change line 452 to: "`matches : a -> Hashed a -> Bool` hashes its **left-hand** argument under the policy recorded on the right-hand stored value and compares in constant time." Apply the identical rewrite to the sentence at docs/auth.md:238-239. Leave all six call sites as written.
- **Verifier note:** Reproduced by reading all six call sites; every one puts the plaintext on the left. No superseding note in open-questions.md (OQ-037 covers Encrypted, not the signature).

### [major] `Pending` is simultaneously a built-in `Null`-derived absence type and an ordinary domain variant in five examples, including the scheduler's own state machine

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:320, docs/events.md:78, docs/events.md:279, docs/events.md:573, docs/schema/traits.md:312, docs/cli.md:330, docs/schema/queries.md:565, docs/category-model.md:162, docs/connectors.md:81
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md
- **Evidence:** types.md:320 lists `| `Pending` | Not yet computed or arrived |` in the table headed "Built-in absence types (all extend `Null`)", and traits.md:33 uses it that way (`claimed_at : Timestamp | Pending`). Against that: events.md:78 `status : Pending | Shipped | Cancelled = Pending`; cli.md:330 `status : Pending | Processing | Shipped | Cancelled = Pending`; events.md:279 and traits.md:312 `disposition : Pending | InFlight | Done | Failed`; events.md:573 "Selects queue rows whose `state.disposition is Pending`"; queries.md:565 `{ …, status = Pending }`.
- **Why it is wrong:** One name is bound to two concepts and the consequences are mechanical. Under the head rule (schema/README.md:143-152) the head of `Pending | Shipped | Cancelled` decides the token, and `Pending` extends `Null`. railroad.md:313 then rejects `unique { status }` on any of these fields; queries.md:89-90 makes `Null`-derived types "always match, so they serve as the catch-all", so `>< Order | Pending` silently becomes an outer join; tables.md:207 rejects the field from a candidate key; and OQ-005:379 degenerates the derived key of any projection carrying it. The `disposition` case is the worst, because it is DataCode's own scheduler state.
- **Fix:** Rename the built-in, which has one call site and no examples depending on the name: change types.md:320 to `| `NotYetComputed` | Not yet computed or arrived |`, update traits.md:33 to `claimed_at : Timestamp | NotYetComputed`, and update the absence list in category-model.md:162. Add one line under types.md's absence table: reusing a built-in absence name as an ordinary variant changes key eligibility and join behaviour, so the linter rejects it. Record the rename as a bullet under OQ-005.

### [major] The grain alignment order is stated in full in three files, and "forest" mis-describes a DAG in which `Day` has two parents

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:255-280, docs/schema/aggregates.md:114-144, docs/schema/railroad.md:361-369, docs/open-questions.md:377
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md
- **Evidence:** types.md:257-264: "Every grain declares the grain it **aligns into** … and that forms a forest rather than a total order:" with `Minute → Hour → Day → Month → Quarter → Year` / `Day → IsoWeek → IsoYear`, "Two roots". aggregates.md:116-144 repeats the diagram, the January-29 straddling-week argument, the declared-not-computed argument, and the ISO-year labelling rule with `bucket_start` as the Monday. railroad.md:361-369 states the chain and the maximum-span rule a third time. types.md:274 links forward to aggregates.md#grain-order "for the retention consequence" while restating that consequence itself.
- **Why it is wrong:** Three normative copies of one rule, already worded differently enough that an edit to one will not obviously require touching the others. The description is also wrong: `Day` has two outgoing alignment edges, so a grain does not declare "the" grain it aligns into and the structure is a DAG with a shared node and two maximal elements, not a forest — and "two roots" names the two sinks. This matters because railroad.md:361 requires each step's grain to be "the **alignment parent**" of its predecessor's, which is ill-defined with two parents; the check must be reachability along alignment edges.
- **Fix:** Make docs/schema/types.md#grains-align-they-do-not-merely-coarsen the single home. There, replace "forest"/"two roots" with: "Alignment forms a DAG — `Day` aligns into both `Month` and `IsoWeek`, giving two maximal grains, `Year` and `IsoYear`. A step is admissible where its grain is reachable from its predecessor's along alignment edges." Reduce docs/schema/aggregates.md:114-144 to the two retention consequences (maximum-span comparison, ISO-week labelling) with a link, and reduce railroad.md:361-369 to a one-line bullet plus a link. Fix "alignment parent" to "reachable along alignment edges".

### [major] `matches`'s declared signature is reversed relative to every call site, and the prose is wrong for the infix form the docs mandate

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:452, docs/auth.md:238-239, docs/schema/types.md:449, docs/schema/functions.md:103, docs/schema/README.md:188, docs/schema/queries.md:339, docs/auth.md:232
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Evidence:** types.md:452 — "`matches : Hashed a -> a -> Bool` hashes its right-hand argument under the stored policy and compares in constant time." auth.md:238-239 — "`matches` hashes its right-hand argument under the policy recorded on the stored value". Every call site is infix with the plaintext first: types.md:449 and functions.md:103 ``attempt `matches` user.password``; README.md:188 ``attempt `matches` credential.secret``; queries.md:339 ``attempt `matches` u.password``; auth.md:232 ``attempt `matches` c.secret``. railroad.md:551-553 — backtick infix is Haskell's, so ``x `f` y`` is `f x y`.
- **Why it is wrong:** Under `Hashed a -> a -> Bool`, ``attempt `matches` user.password`` binds `attempt` (the plaintext) to the `Hashed a` slot and `user.password` (the stored digest) to the `a` slot — the reverse of what every example means. auth.md:239 compounds it: "hashes its right-hand argument under the policy recorded on the stored value" is self-contradictory, because in the infix form the right-hand argument *is* the stored value.
- **Fix:** In docs/schema/types.md#comparison change line 452 to "`matches : a -> Hashed a -> Bool` hashes its **left-hand** argument under the policy recorded with its right-hand one and compares in constant time." Change auth.md:238-239 to match. Leave all six call sites unchanged.
- **Verifier note:** Merged two duplicate candidates.

### [major] `matches` is declared with its arguments in the opposite order from every call site, and auth.md's prose says the stored digest is what gets hashed

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:449-453, docs/auth.md:232, docs/auth.md:238-240, docs/schema/queries.md:333-339, docs/schema/railroad.md:551-557, docs/schema/README.md:188
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#comparison
- **Evidence:** types.md:452: "`matches : Hashed a -> a -> Bool` hashes its right-hand argument under the stored policy and compares in constant time." Every call site puts the plaintext on the left: auth.md:232 ``attempt `matches` c.secret``, types.md:449 and railroad.md:556 ``attempt `matches` user.password``, queries.md:339 ``attempt `matches` u.password``, README.md:188 ``attempt `matches` credential.secret``. railroad.md:551-553 fixes backtick infix as Haskell's ``x `f` y == f x y``. auth.md:238-240: "`matches` hashes its **right-hand** argument under the policy recorded on the stored value".
- **Why it is wrong:** Under the declared signature, ``attempt `matches` c.secret`` requires `attempt : Hashed a` and `c.secret : a` — the exact inverse of what the values are, so every call site in the corpus is ill-typed. auth.md:238-240 compounds it: with the plaintext on the left the "right-hand argument" *is* the stored digest, so the sentence describes hashing an already-hashed value under a policy recorded on itself, which never verifies. Only queries.md:334 ("hashes **the attempt** once per row") is cryptographically right.
- **Fix:** In types.md#comparison, change the signature to `matches : a -> Hashed a -> Bool` and the sentence to "hashes its **left-hand** argument under the policy recorded on the stored value on its right, and compares in constant time." Delete the restatement at auth.md:237-241 and replace it with a link to types.md#comparison.

### [major] `matches`'s declared signature and prose are the reverse of all five call sites

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:452, docs/auth.md:239, docs/schema/types.md:449, docs/schema/queries.md:339, docs/schema/functions.md:103, docs/schema/README.md:188
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#comparison
- **Evidence:** types.md:452 "`matches : Hashed a -> a -> Bool` hashes its right-hand argument under the stored policy and compares in constant time." auth.md:239 repeats it: "`matches` hashes its right-hand argument under the policy recorded on the stored value." Every call site puts the plaintext on the left: types.md:449 ``attempt `matches` user.password``; queries.md:339 ``in  attempt `matches` u.password``; functions.md:103 ``attempt `matches` user.password``; README.md:188 ``attempt `matches` credential.secret``; auth.md:232 ``attempt `matches` c.secret``.
- **Why it is wrong:** ``x `matches` y`` means `matches x y`, so the call sites pass the *attempt* first and the stored `Hashed` value second — the opposite of `Hashed a -> a -> Bool`, and the opposite of "hashes its right-hand argument" (the right-hand argument at every call site is the stored digest, which is already hashed). One of the two is wrong, and since the infix reading is what makes the assertion read naturally, the signature is the one to change.
- **Fix:** Change types.md:452 to `matches : a -> Hashed a -> Bool` and reword to "hashes its **left**-hand argument under the policy recorded on the right-hand stored value". Update auth.md:239 identically. Leave the call sites alone.

### [major] `|` is described as a relational union operator that the language does not have

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:79-80, docs/schema/queries.md:460, docs/schema/queries.md:481-485, docs/open-questions.md:397, docs/schema/railroad.md:1019-1022
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/queries.md
- **Evidence:** types.md:79 "The `|` operator builds sum types. This is the same operator used for **relational union** — context (type-annotation position vs. query-expression position) disambiguates." queries.md:460 lists a key-propagation row "`\|` union | The source key **plus a discriminator**, which may not exist". Against this, OQ-005 (open-questions.md:397) records "`union`, `except`, `intersect`, `window`, `over`, and `partition` are consequently unreserved" and railroad.md:1019 records union as considered and **not** reserved.
- **Why it is wrong:** No production in `Query`/`QueryClause` admits a binary union of two queries. In query position `|` appears only inside `JoinSource ::= TypeExpr | '(' Query ')' ( '|' TypeExpr )*`, where it is outer-join *guard alternation*, not union — guard alternation picks one variant per row, union concatenates row sets. Documenting key propagation for a nonexistent operator, under a spelling that means something else, will send an implementer looking for a production that was deliberately never added.
- **Fix:** Delete the "relational union" clause from types.md:79 (say `|` is sum-type alternation and outer-join guard alternation). In queries.md:460 and 481, either drop the union row or relabel it as the *rollup union generated by a `retain` chain*, which is the only union in the system, and link to aggregates.md#the-union.

### [major] `matches`'s declared signature is the reverse of every use of it

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:449-453, docs/auth.md:232, docs/auth.md:238-239, docs/schema/README.md:188, docs/schema/queries.md:339, docs/schema/railroad.md:556
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#hashed-types
- **Evidence:** types.md:452 declares "`matches : Hashed a -> a -> Bool` hashes its right-hand argument under the stored policy and compares in constant time." auth.md:238 repeats "`matches` hashes its right-hand argument under the policy recorded on the stored value". Every call site puts the plaintext first: types.md:449 and railroad.md:556 `attempt \`matches\` user.password`; README.md:188 `attempt \`matches\` credential.secret`; queries.md:339 `attempt \`matches\` u.password`; auth.md:232 `attempt \`matches\` c.secret`.
- **Why it is wrong:** Backtick infix means `x \`f\` y == f x y`, so `attempt \`matches\` user.password` is `matches attempt user.password`, which types as `a -> Hashed a -> Bool`. The declared signature `Hashed a -> a -> Bool` would require `user.password \`matches\` attempt`. Under the declared signature the "right-hand argument" in every example is the *stored digest*, so auth.md:238's prose would have the runtime re-hashing a digest.
- **Fix:** Change types.md:452 to `matches : a -> Hashed a -> Bool` and reword both prose sentences to "hashes its **left**-hand argument under the policy recorded on the stored value". Leave the call sites unchanged.

### [major] `app.billing.Loan`'s candidate key `loanRef` is declared with two different field lists

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:117-127, docs/schema/tables.md:290-299, docs/schema/tables.md:164, docs/events.md:114
- **Evidence:** types.md:117-127 declares `table app.billing.Loan : UserData { customer :> Customer, account : AccountNumber, principal, rate, opened_at, unique loanRef { customer, account }, balance : Behavior Amount = … }`. tables.md:290-299 declares the same table with no `account` field and `unique loanRef { customer, opened_at }`.
- **Why it is wrong:** Two files give the same table the same constraint name with different columns, and one of them keys on a field the other does not declare. A reader cannot tell which is intended, and the choice matters — `{customer, opened_at}` keys on a `Timestamp` (two loans opened in the same millisecond collide) while `{customer, account}` keys on a business identifier. The same drift appears with `lineRef`: tables.md:164 uses `unique lineRef { customer, order_num }` while events.md:114 uses `unique lineRef { customer, opened_at }`.
- **Fix:** Pick one shape for `Loan` (recommend `{ customer, account }`) and make tables.md:290-299 match types.md:117-127. Rename tables.md:164's example constraint from `lineRef` to `orderRef` — it keys `{customer, order_num}`, which is the Order key everywhere else.

### [minor] `Pending` is both a built-in `Null`-derived absence type and an ordinary domain variant in three sum types

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:320, docs/schema/traits.md:312, docs/events.md:279, docs/cli.md:330, docs/schema/traits.md:33, docs/schema/railroad.md:313, docs/schema/tables.md:207
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#absence-types
- **Evidence:** types.md:314-320 lists `Pending` among the built-in absence types "(all extend `Null`)", meaning "Not yet computed or arrived". traits.md:33 `claimed_at : Timestamp | Pending` uses the absence reading, correctly. traits.md:312 and events.md:279 `disposition : Pending | InFlight | Done | Failed`, cli.md:330 `status : Pending | Processing | Shipped | Cancelled = Pending`, and queries.md:561 `status = Pending` use it as an ordinary domain variant.
- **Why it is wrong:** One name, two concepts, and the collision has consequences. If `Pending` is `Null`-derived then `disposition` and `status` are absence-bearing alternations, which railroad.md:313 and tables.md:207 reject from any key and queries.md degenerates an outer join over; and under README.md:143's head rule, `disposition`'s declared type is rooted at absence, so a queued-but-not-started item types as "this value is missing" rather than "this item is waiting". Every consumer written against the no-NULL discipline reads it wrong.
- **Fix:** Rename the domain variants: `Queued` for the queue disposition (docs/schema/traits.md:312 and docs/events.md:279) and `Placed` for order status (docs/cli.md:330, docs/schema/queries.md:561, and the example in CLAUDE.md). Add a bullet to docs/schema/types.md#absence-types stating that the built-in absence names are reserved against reuse as ordinary variants, since nothing in the position distinguishes them.

### [minor] `FunctorRef`, `EventRef`, `TableRef`, `FormatRef`, `Html` and a list type are used in normative declarations and defined nowhere

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:10-24, docs/schema/functors.md:17, docs/api.md:42-44, docs/api.md:55, docs/integrity.md:205, docs/events.md:184, docs/schema/functions.md:169, docs/schema/templates.md:114-116
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md
- **Evidence:** types.md:10-24 lists the primitives: `Text`, `Int`, `Decimal`, `Bool`, `Date`, `Timestamp`, `Duration`, `Period`, `Grain`, `Moment`, `Bytes`, `DataId`, `Doc`. But integrity.md:205 declares `functor : FunctorRef`, events.md:184 `trigger : FunctorRef`, api.md:42-44 `table_ref : TableRef unique` / `methods : [HttpMethod]` / `format_ref : FormatRef`, functors.md:17 gives the event signature as `a → EventRef`, and functions.md:169 writes `type Renderer = Amount -> Read Html`.
- **Why it is wrong:** Six types appear in system-table declarations and functor signatures with no definition. An implementer cannot say what a `FunctorRef` holds (a `DataId` into the schema graph? a content hash?), whether `EventRef` is a row identity or a queue coordinate, or whether `Html` is a `Secret`-like opaque wrapper or a `Text` refinement. `Html` is load-bearing for the injection-safety claim at templates.md:114-116, which rests entirely on `Html` being unconstructible except by a template or render function — a property no declaration states. `[HttpMethod]` is worse than undefined: `TypeExpr ::= Variant ( '|' Variant )*` with `Variant ::= QName TypeArg* | '(' TypeExpr ( ',' TypeExpr )+ ')'` admits no `[ ]`, so api.md:43 does not parse.
- **Fix:** Add a "System types" section to schema/types.md declaring `FunctorRef`, `EventRef`, `TableRef` and `Html`, each with its underlying representation and its construction restriction (state explicitly that `Html` has no literal form and is produced only by a template or a render function), and link to it from functors.md, api.md, integrity.md and templates.md. Either add a list production to railroad.md's `TypeExpr` or rewrite api.md:43 as a `Component` sub-table of methods; either way replace `FormatRef` at api.md:44 with `:> system.api.FormatFunctor`.

### [minor] `Sealed` and `Redacted` are read-time variants that appear in no field's declared type

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:371, docs/schema/types.md:484, docs/schema/functors.md:112, docs/schema/types.md:338, docs/schema/README.md:143
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#secret-types
- **Evidence:** types.md:371 "Reads | The field resolves to `Sealed`, a `Null`-derived absence type. Never to the stored bytes, for any token." types.md:484-485 "An `Encrypted` field reads as `Sealed` for every token." functors.md:112 "On failure, read | … row resolves to `Redacted`". Against types.md:338-343 ("Using absence types in fields: `phone : Phone | NotGiven` — reason for absence is typed") and README.md:143-145's head rule.
- **Why it is wrong:** Everywhere else an absence a reader can encounter is written into the field's declared type — that is the whole content of "no NULL, absence is typed". These two are the exceptions: `secret : TotpSecret` reads as `Sealed` and any field under a failing access assert reads as `Redacted`, and neither variant appears in any declaration. A client generating types from `:describe` gets the wrong sum for every `Secret` field and every access-constrained field, and nothing says whether `secret is Sealed` typechecks given the declared type has no such variant.
- **Fix:** Add to docs/schema/types.md#secret-types: "A `Secret` field's declared type is `T`; its **read** type is `Sealed`. The variant is supplied by the system, never declared, and `is Sealed` is admissible on any such field." Add the parallel sentence for `T | Redacted` to docs/schema/constraints.md's redaction section, and state in both that `:describe` and generated API types report the read type.

### [minor] There is no syntax for marking a type `Secret`, yet four commit-time rules hang off the marking

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:363, docs/schema/types.md:367, docs/schema/railroad.md:90, docs/schema/railroad.md:1033
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#secret-types
- **Evidence:** types.md:363 "A type may be marked **`Secret`**. This is a property of the type, not a functor and not an access rule"; types.md:367 "Marking a type `Secret` has four effects, all enforced at schema commit". `TypeDecl` (railroad.md:90) has no slot for a marker; `Secret` is absent from the reserved-word list (railroad.md:879-893) and from the list of ordinary identifiers at railroad.md:1033-1035, which names `Hashed` and `Encrypted` but not `Secret`.
- **Why it is wrong:** "A type may be marked" reads as a general capability, but the only routes to `Secret` are the two built-in constructors. An author wanting `Secret` on a recovery code stored as `Bytes` or a bearer token has no spelling, and the doc gives no signal that this is intended. Four commit-time rules attach to a property with no declaration form.
- **Fix:** Rewrite the opener of docs/schema/types.md#secret-types as: "A type built with `Hashed` or `Encrypted` is **`Secret`**. There is no user-applicable marker — `Secret` names the property those two constructors carry." If user-marked secrets are wanted instead, add the modifier to `TypeDecl` in railroad.md:90 and reserve the word.

### [minor] "A field whose type is X" is never true under the field-scoped-subtype rule, so several structural checks are vacuous as literally written

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:68, docs/schema/traits.md:303, docs/schema/traits.md:306, docs/schema/railroad.md:165, docs/schema/railroad.md:312, docs/schema/railroad.md:284
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#domain-types
- **Evidence:** types.md:68-71 "When a field in a table references a domain type, it creates a new named subtype scoped to that field (`namespace.table.field`) … Two fields in different tables are always distinct types even if they share the same domain type as their parent." traits.md:303 "At most **one** field whose type is `Priority`"; traits.md:306 "Rules 2 and 3 read the field's **type**, never its name." railroad.md:165 "rejected on a field whose type is `Secret`"; railroad.md:312 "may not name a field whose type is `Secret`, `Doc`, `Behavior`, a function type".
- **Why it is wrong:** Under the scoping rule, `urgency : Priority` on a queue has type `app.auth.LdapSync.urgency`, whose *parent* is `Priority`. Type identity with `Priority`, `Secret`, `Doc`, or `Behavior` is therefore never true of any field, so every rule phrased as "the field whose type is X" fires zero times as literally written. The intended test is ancestry in the domain-type chain, which is strictly weaker and needs saying — particularly for `Secret`, where an author could otherwise appear to shed the property by wrapping a `Hashed` type in one more `type` declaration.
- **Fix:** Add one sentence to docs/schema/types.md#domain-types: "Every rule elsewhere phrased as *a field whose type is `X`* means *whose computed field type has `X` in its ancestor chain*; a field-scoped subtype never compares equal to its parent." Add a second sentence stating that `Secret`, `Behavior`, `Doc`-ness and function-typeness are inherited down the chain and cannot be shed by a further `type` declaration. Leave the individual rules as written.

### [minor] A `Behavior a`'s body is ill-typed against its declared element type, and that type's predicates can never run

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:126, docs/schema/types.md:242, docs/schema/types.md:292, docs/schema/types.md:37, docs/schema/functors.md:51, docs/schema/tables.md:298, docs/schema/traits.md:431
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#behaviors
- **Evidence:** types.md:126 `balance : Behavior Amount = \t -> principal * (1 + rate * (t - opened_at) / day)`, with `type Amount : Decimal where \a -> a >= 0` (types.md:37). types.md:242-243: "arithmetic operates on `Decimal` and the result widens back to it." types.md:292 rejects `where` on a behavior field: "The predicate would have to hold at every moment, which is undecidable in general." functors.md:51 "1. **Coerce** the supplied value to the field's declared type" — step 1 of the order of operations *for a field write*.
- **Why it is wrong:** By the widening rule the lambda has type `Moment -> Decimal`, not `Moment -> Amount`, and nothing states a narrowing rule for a behavior. The only coercion the docs define is step 1 of the field-write path, and a behavior has no write. So `Behavior Amount` promises `a >= 0`, no functor ever checks it, and a negative `principal` or `rate` yields a negative `Amount`. The same expression is repeated verbatim in three files (types.md:126, tables.md:298, traits.md:431), so it is the load-bearing example for the whole feature.
- **Fix:** Add to docs/schema/types.md#behaviors: "A behavior's body is checked against the *parent primitive* of its declared element type. Because no functor runs on a read, a declared element type carrying `where` predicates is rejected — those predicates could not be enforced. Constrain the stored fields the behavior closes over instead." Then change the three examples to `balance : Behavior Decimal`, or keep `Amount` and state the observation-time check and what a failure resolves to.

### [minor] The grain alignment structure is a DAG with one source, not "a forest with two roots", and `Day` has two alignment parents

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:257, docs/schema/types.md:266, docs/schema/aggregates.md:117, docs/schema/aggregates.md:124, docs/schema/railroad.md:361
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#grains-align-they-do-not-merely-coarsen
- **Evidence:** types.md:257-259 "Every grain declares the grain it **aligns into** — the one whose buckets its own buckets tile exactly — and that forms a forest rather than a total order", followed by `Minute → Hour → Day → Month → Quarter → Year` / `                Day → IsoWeek → IsoYear` and types.md:266 "Two roots". aggregates.md:117 and :124 repeat both. railroad.md:361-362 "Each step's grain must be the **alignment parent** of its predecessor's, transitively — `Minute → … → Year` **or** `Day → IsoWeek → IsoYear`."
- **Why it is wrong:** In the drawn structure `Day` aligns into both `Month` and `IsoWeek`. A forest is a disjoint union of trees, in which every node has at most one parent; this is a rooted DAG with a single source (`Minute`) and two maximal elements (`Year`, `IsoYear`). Three consequences the wording gets wrong: "the one whose buckets its own tile exactly" and "the alignment parent" are stated as functions and are not, so an implementer building a parent pointer gets `Day` wrong; "two roots" names the maximal elements while the single source is `Minute`; and railroad.md's "or" reads as two disjoint total orders, under which `by Hour , by Day , by IsoWeek` — legal by reachability — is unresolved.
- **Fix:** In docs/schema/types.md#grains-align-they-do-not-merely-coarsen, replace "forms a forest rather than a total order" with "forms a rooted DAG — a partial order given by its covering relation — rather than a total order", replace "Two roots" with "One source, `Minute`; two maximal grains, `Year` and `IsoYear`; `Day` aligns into two", and restate the chain rule as "each step's grain must be reachable from its predecessor's along alignment edges". Mirror the wording at aggregates.md:117-128, and at railroad.md:361-362 replace "or" with the branch-at-`Day` reading plus the consequence that a chain may cross into the ISO branch at `Day` but never back.

### [minor] `table app.billing.Loan` is declared with incompatible bodies in types.md and tables.md, including two different `loanRef` keys

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:117, docs/schema/types.md:124, docs/schema/tables.md:290, docs/schema/tables.md:296, docs/schema/traits.md:434
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#behaviors
- **Evidence:** types.md:117-127: `table app.billing.Loan : UserData { customer :> Customer, account : AccountNumber, principal, rate, opened_at, unique loanRef { customer, account }, balance : Behavior Amount = … }`. tables.md:290-299: the same table with no `account` field and `unique loanRef { customer, opened_at }`. traits.md:434 gives a third shape, `table app.billing.Loan : Accruing, UserData { customer :> Customer, ... }`, with the fields supplied by the trait.
- **Why it is wrong:** One fully-qualified table, one named constraint, two different attribute sets, in two normative files. The elision disclaimer at tables.md:226 covers *omitting* a key, not changing one. `unique loanRef { customer, opened_at }` is also materially worse: it makes loan identity depend on a timestamp, so two loans opened in the same millisecond collide.
- **Fix:** Make docs/schema/traits.md:426-435's `Accruing` form canonical (it supplies `principal`/`rate`/`opened_at`), fix docs/schema/tables.md:290-299 to use `unique loanRef { customer, account }` with the `account : AccountNumber` field present, and have docs/schema/types.md:117-127 match it verbatim.

### [minor] The grain alignment forest and its two consequences are stated in full in three files

The copies have already begun to drift: the max-span example is `for 30 day` in railroad.md and types.md and appears as both `for 30 day` (rejected) and `for 31 day` (accepted) in aggregates.md, and only types.md carries the `isoWeekOf` pair.

### [minor] `HashPolicy`'s flat parameter set fits Argon2id only; two of its three algorithms have no use for three of its columns

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:421, docs/schema/types.md:89
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#policies
- **Evidence:** types.md:421-428: `table system.crypto.HashPolicy : Reference { name : Text unique, algorithm : Argon2id | Scrypt | Bcrypt, memory_kib : Int, iterations : Int, parallelism : Int, salt_bytes : Int }`.
- **Why it is wrong:** The four parameter columns are Argon2id's (m, t, p, salt). Bcrypt takes a single cost factor and a fixed 128-bit salt, so `memory_kib`, `iterations`, and `parallelism` are meaningless for it and `salt_bytes` is not adjustable. Scrypt takes N (a cost parameter, not an iteration count), r (block size, not memory in KiB), and p — all three misnamed here. In a language whose central claim is that the *reason* for absence lives in the type, three of six columns are silently inapplicable for two of three variants, with no `NotApplicable` variant and no assert relating `algorithm` to the parameter set. `salt_bytes` also carries no minimum.
- **Fix:** In docs/schema/types.md#policies, give `algorithm` a payload carrying its own parameters — `algorithm : Argon2id ArgonParams | Scrypt ScryptParams | Bcrypt BcryptCost` — which the payload-carrying sum types at types.md:89-93 already support, and drop the four flat columns. Put a `where \n -> n >= 16` on whichever salt field survives and cite NIST SP 800-63B §5.1.1.2 for the floor.

### [minor] `FunctorRef`, `TypeRef`, and `Row` are used as types throughout and declared nowhere

- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED

Uses: `FunctorRef` in api.md:55, api.md:71-75, integrity.md:205, events.md:184; `TypeRef` in events.md:385-386, events.md:525, auth.md:305; `Row` in functors.md:15-16, category-model.md:40, integrity.md:223, and — as a first-class DataCode type on the left of an arrow in a `TypeDecl` — functions.md:170 (`type LineFormat = Row -> Read Text`).

- **Fix:** Add `FunctorRef`, `TypeRef`, and `Row t` to docs/schema/types.md#primitive-types with one-line definitions and to railroad.md:1033's list. Change functions.md:170 to a concrete table type (`type LineFormat = app.commerce.OrderLine -> Read Text`) or to the parameterized `Row t`, and keep bare `Row` strictly to signature prose in functors.md and category-model.md.
- **Verifier note:** Merged two duplicate candidates. Noted that railroad.md:1036's list ends in an ellipsis, so its silence is weaker evidence than types.md's.

### [minor] The `Secret` predicate-signature restriction is stated normatively in four files, and the stated reason is wrong for `a -> Maybe b`

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:372, docs/schema/types.md:376-379, docs/schema/functors.md:92-98, docs/schema/functions.md:92-95, docs/integrity.md:273-276
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Evidence:** types.md:372 — "Only `a -> Bool` is admitted. `a -> Either Error a` and `a -> Maybe b` are rejected." types.md:376-379 gives the reason for `Either` only: "an author writing `\p -> Left (Error ("rejected: " <> p))` would put a credential into the append-only log". functors.md:94-98 and functions.md:92-95 both generalise it: "because **their failure channels** can carry the value itself out into an error payload". integrity.md:273-276 states it a fourth time.
- **Why it is wrong:** `Maybe`'s failure channel is `Nothing`, which carries nothing — there is no error payload to leak through. The real reason to reject `a -> Maybe b` on a `Secret` field is that its *success* channel returns a value of a different type `b`, so it is a transform rather than a predicate, and a transform whose output is not `Secret` would launder the plaintext out through the value channel. Stating a reason demonstrably false for one of the two rejected signatures is worse than stating none. types.md, the home, is the one of the four that gets it right — evidence the other three are drifted restatements.
- **Fix:** Keep the rule and rationale in docs/schema/types.md#secret-types and add the `Maybe` reason there: "`a -> Maybe b` is rejected on different grounds — its success channel returns a different type, so it is a transform rather than a predicate, and would carry the plaintext out through the value channel." Reduce functors.md:92-98, functions.md:92-95, and integrity.md:273-276 to one sentence plus the existing link.
- **Verifier note:** Merged two duplicate candidates.

### [minor] `FunctorRef`, `TypeRef`, and `system.integrity.Mode` are used normatively and defined nowhere

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:10-24, docs/integrity.md:170, docs/integrity.md:205, docs/auth.md:305, docs/events.md:184, docs/api.md:71-75
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#primitive-types

- **Why it is wrong:** Two column types appear in six files with no normative home stating what they hold, how they compare, whether they survive a `prune` of their target, or what a dangling one reads as. `system.integrity.Mode` is the storage for every enforcement mode in the system and is never declared, so mode precedence — two statements naming one validation, or a field-level and a predicate-level mode — is unspecified with it.

Declare `system.integrity.Mode` in integrity.md#declaring-a-mode alongside `Violation`, with the precedence rule for overlapping statements.

### [minor] `Behavior a ≅ Moment -> a` asserts an isomorphism the closed-form restriction contradicts

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:105-110, docs/category-model.md:111-113, docs/category-model.md:122-126
- **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md
- **Evidence:** types.md:109 and category-model.md:111-113 both give `Behavior a  ≅  Moment -> a`. category-model.md:123-125: "An arbitrary `Moment -> a` can be sampled but not solved, and a scheduler that can only sample is a poller. The class is a constraint on the *category*".
- **Why it is wrong:** If behaviors are restricted to a closed-form-solvable class, `Behavior a` is a proper subset of `Moment -> a` and the two are not isomorphic. The distinction is the standard one in push-pull FRP: `Moment -> a` is the denotation, and the admissible representations are deliberately narrower so they can be solved. Written as `≅`, two statements in the same document contradict each other and the one an implementer would build against is the wrong one.
- **Fix:** Change both occurrences to a denotation rather than an isomorphism — `⟦Behavior a⟧ : Moment -> a` — and add after each: "the denotation is total; the admissible representations are restricted to a closed-form-solvable class so the scheduler can solve for a crossing (OQ-034)."

### [minor] Hash-policy rotation is specified as `enforce forward`, but no `ValidationRef` can address a type's storage transform

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:437, docs/schema/railroad.md:431, docs/schema/railroad.md:434, docs/schema/functors.md:56, docs/schema/functors.md:80
- **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#rotation
- **Evidence:** types.md:437-440 "Changing the policy is repointing the type at a new policy row — a schema commit against a populated field, which … must declare an enforcement mode. The mode is `enforce forward`: existing digests keep working, and every row hashed under the superseded policy becomes a reportable violation." railroad.md:431 `ValidationRef ::= QName ( '/' Ident )?` and :434-436 "`ValidationRef` addresses a validation by the path that already names it … An `assert` is addressed by its own name." functors.md:52-58 puts validation at step 2 and the type's storage transform at step 4.
- **Why it is wrong:** A `using` repoint alters step 4, not step 2, so there is no term naming "the hash transform on `app.auth.User.password`" and no way to write the mandatory statement. Nor does the enforcement-mode table (functors.md:80-85) define what a *transform* violation is: `enforce forward` there means "reject the violating write, record pre-existing violators", but after a rotation every existing digest is a violator by construction, so the rotation raises one violation row per credential rather than the reportable-set semantics types.md:440 describes.
- **Fix:** Pick one and record it under OQ-037. Either extend `ValidationRef` in docs/schema/railroad.md:431 to address a field's transform (`app.auth.User.password / policy`) and add a transform-mismatch row to functors.md's enforcement-mode table; or state in docs/schema/types.md#rotation that a `using` repoint is not an enforcement-mode-bearing change and that superseded-policy values are surfaced by a standing query over the policy tag recorded on each value, not by the violations table.
- **Verifier note:** The narrow claim is confirmed — no production names a transform, and the mode table has no transform row. It is arguable that `enforce app.auth.User.password forward` (no `/`) addresses the field's computed type and so reaches the transform; the docs do not say, which is the defect.

### [minor] `Moment` is said to range over the future, but the only way to supply one also selects a graph position

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:150, docs/schema/queries.md:352, docs/schema/queries.md:390, docs/schema/railroad.md:622, docs/schema/railroad.md:680
- **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/queries.md#every-query-has-a-sample-moment
- **Evidence:** types.md:150-152 "`Moment` also ranges over the past and the future … the scheduler evaluates one at future moments to find when a condition *will* become true." railroad.md:622 `AtClause ::= 'at' StringLit`; railroad.md:680-682 "`AtClause`'s `StringLit` is a version token … or an ISO-8601 moment; the two are told apart at resolution." queries.md:394-395 "`balance` has no value except at a moment, and the query supplies the moment instead of the field fetching it."
- **Why it is wrong:** `at` is one knob selecting both the row version and the `Moment` argument. For a past moment that is coherent; for a future one it is not, because no graph state exists there, and nothing says whether `Loan at "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z" { balance }` is rejected, clamped to HEAD, or resolves rows at HEAD while passing the future moment to the behavior. The scheduler is described as doing the last of these, so the capability exists internally with no user-facing spelling, and "project this balance 30 days out" — the first question anyone asks of a `Behavior` — has no stated answer. OQ-034 does not cover it; it is about solving for crossings, not sampling.
- **Fix:** State the choice in docs/schema/queries.md#every-query-has-a-sample-moment and record it under OQ-005: either a future `at` moment is legal and means "rows as of HEAD, behaviors evaluated at M" (with the non-reproducibility called out), or future moments are rejected in `at` and a per-projection sampling form (`balance at M as projected_balance`) makes row version and observation moment independent knobs.

### [minor] `app.billing.Loan` is declared three incompatible ways in three files

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:117, docs/schema/tables.md:290, docs/schema/traits.md:434
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#behaviors
- **Evidence:** types.md:117-127 declares `Loan` with `customer`, `account : AccountNumber`, `principal`, `rate`, `opened_at`, `unique loanRef { customer, account }`, and `balance` defined inline. tables.md:290-299 declares the same table with no `account` field and `unique loanRef { customer, opened_at }`. traits.md:434 declares `table app.billing.Loan : Accruing, UserData { customer :> Customer, ... }`, taking `principal`/`rate`/`opened_at`/`balance` from a trait and declaring no key at all.
- **Why it is wrong:** Three declarations of one fully-qualified table with three different key definitions under one constraint name, and two different sources for `balance`. queries.md:356 then queries `Loan at "2026-03-01T00:00:00Z" { account, balance }`, which only types against the types.md version. tables.md:228's elision disclaimer covers omitted keys, not two *different* declared keys for the same named constraint.
- **Fix:** Make types.md:117 the single declaration (it is the most complete), have tables.md:290 and traits.md:434 present fragments that agree with it — tables.md keeping `unique loanRef { customer, account }`, traits.md showing only the trait-derived fields — and add a one-line pointer from each to the full version.

### [minor] `Pending` names both a built-in `Null`-derived absence type and an ordinary status variant in four places

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:321, docs/schema/tables.md:14, docs/cli.md:330, docs/events.md:78, docs/schema/traits.md:311, docs/schema/queries.md:565
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#absence-types
- **Evidence:** types.md:321 lists `Pending` among the built-in absence types ("all extend `Null`") with meaning "Not yet computed or arrived". Used as an ordinary variant: cli.md:330 `status    : Pending | Processing | Shipped | Cancelled = Pending`; events.md:78 `status    : Pending | Shipped | Cancelled = Pending`; traits.md:311/events.md:279 `disposition : Pending | InFlight | Done | Failed`; queries.md:565 `{ ..., status = Pending }`. traits.md:34 also uses it as a value type: `claimed_at : Timestamp | Pending`.
- **Why it is wrong:** One name carries two concepts with different consequences. Because `Pending` extends `Null`, tables.md:207 rejects any key containing a field typed with it, queries.md:488 makes outer joins over it degenerate the derived key, and `phone is NotGiven`-style absence handling applies — none of which is wanted for an order status or a queue disposition. The `Order` key `{customer, order_num}` is unaffected only by luck; a table keyed on `status` would be silently rejected for a reason its author could not read off the declaration.
- **Fix:** Rename the status/disposition variants: `Placed` (order), `Queued` (disposition). Alternatively rename the absence type to `NotYetComputed`, but `Pending` reads better as absence and there are only four collision sites. Either way, add a line to types.md#absence-types warning that a built-in absence-type name is not available as an ordinary variant.

### [minor] The `Loan` example is declared twice with different keys and different fields

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:117-127, docs/schema/tables.md:290-299, docs/schema/queries.md:356
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md
- **Evidence:** types.md:119-124 — `account   : AccountNumber,` … `unique loanRef { customer, account },`. tables.md:296 — `unique loanRef { customer, opened_at },` with no `account` field. queries.md:356 — `Loan at "2026-03-01T00:00:00Z" { account, balance }` projects `account`, which exists only in the types.md version.
- **Why it is wrong:** One named table with one named constraint, declared two ways in two normative files, and a third file projecting a field only one of them declares. `{customer, opened_at}` and `{customer, account}` are also different design claims — the first keys a loan by when it opened.
- **Fix:** Declare `app.billing.Loan` once (types.md#behaviors is the natural home, since the behavior is the point) and have tables.md#behavior-fields link to it rather than restate it.

### [nit] Tuple types are declarable but have no literal, no destructuring, and no accessors, so `isoWeekOf` is unusable

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:97, docs/schema/types.md:279, docs/schema/railroad.md:95, docs/schema/railroad.md:482, docs/schema/railroad.md:495
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#product-types
- **Evidence:** types.md:97 "Tuple notation `(A, B)` is available for and-types used outside a named record." railroad.md:94-96 `Variant ::= QName TypeArg* | '(' TypeExpr ( ',' TypeExpr )+ ')'`. types.md:279 "`isoWeekOf :: Timestamp -> (Int, Int)` returns the pair for anyone who wants the number directly." railroad.md:482-497 `Atom` has no tuple alternative, `LetExpr` binds one `Ident`, `Lambda`'s `Param` is an `Ident`.
- **Why it is wrong:** The tuple exists at the type level only. No production writes a tuple value, there is no pattern binding, and there is no `fst`/`snd` or positional projection, so `isoWeekOf`'s result — the documented way to get the ISO year/week pair an `IsoWeek` bucket is labelled by — cannot be consumed by any expression in the language.
- **Fix:** Either add `'(' Expr ( ',' Expr )+ ')'` to `Atom` in docs/schema/railroad.md:482 plus tuple patterns in `LetExpr` and `Lambda`, or replace `isoWeekOf`'s pair with two functions (`isoYearOf`, `isoWeekNumberOf`) at docs/schema/types.md:279 and docs/schema/functions.md:157 and delete tuple notation from types.md#product-types as unimplemented. State the choice in types.md.

### [nit] `reveal` is named as the sole path to `Encrypted` plaintext but has no type signature anywhere

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:484, docs/schema/types.md:493, docs/schema/railroad.md:1030, docs/schema/types.md:452
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#encrypted-types
- **Evidence:** types.md:484-485 "Plaintext is reached only by `reveal`, which runs in `Effect`." types.md:493 "Who may call `reveal` is an ordinary grant." railroad.md:1030 "`reveal` is an ordinary `Effect` function, not a keyword, exactly as `matches` is an ordinary function." `matches` is given a signature at types.md:452; `reveal` is given none.
- **Why it is wrong:** The missing signature is not obvious. `reveal` must take the `Encrypted a` value, but every read of such a field yields `Sealed` (types.md:484), so nothing says how a handler obtains the argument; and it must fail for an ungranted token, so the return is not a bare `a`. An implementer cannot write the handler-side call.
- **Fix:** Add to docs/schema/types.md#decryption-is-an-effect-never-a-read: `reveal : Encrypted a -> Effect (a | Sealed)`, returning `Sealed` where the calling handler's grant does not cover the field, plus one sentence saying how a handler obtains the `Encrypted a` value given that every query read yields `Sealed`.

### [nit] The `Duration`/`Period` operator table lists operand orders the corpus never uses and omits `Duration + Duration`

- **Where:** docs/schema/types.md:164, docs/schema/types.md:165, docs/schema/types.md:210, docs/schema/types.md:220, docs/schema/types.md:230, docs/schema/functions.md:152, docs/schema/railroad.md:345
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md#moment-is-not-timestamp
- **Evidence:** types.md:164-165 lists `Duration * Decimal | Duration` and `Period * Int | Period`. Every use writes the scalar first: types.md:210 "`7 * day`, `2 * week`", types.md:219 "`now + 3 * month`", types.md:230 "`d + 3 * month`", functions.md:152 "`signed_at + 3 * month`", railroad.md:345 "`7 day` is `7 * day`".
- **Why it is wrong:** The table gives type rules for `Duration * Decimal` and `Period * Int`; every actual expression in the corpus is the reverse. Commutativity is stated nowhere, and since `Duration`, `Period`, and `Decimal` are distinct types rather than one numeric type, the checker needs both directions declared. `Duration + Duration` and `Duration - Duration` are also absent, though `1 * day + 6 * hour` is the obvious way to build a composite length under "units are values".
- **Fix:** Add four rows to the table at docs/schema/types.md:154-165 — `Decimal * Duration | Duration`, `Int * Period | Period`, `Duration + Duration | Duration`, `Duration - Duration | Duration` — and one sentence stating that scalar multiplication commutes while `Period` and `Duration` never mix.

## docs/namespaces.md

31 findings — 1 blocker, 15 major, 14 minor, 1 nit.

### [blocker] `namespace app.commerce` is not a production, is not reserved, and contradicts "no explicit creation syntax"

- **Where:** docs/namespaces.md:57-68, docs/schema/railroad.md:69-81, docs/schema/railroad.md:876-893, docs/schema/README.md:70-71
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/railroad.md (grammar); docs/namespaces.md (the example)
- **Evidence:** namespaces.md:57 — "Namespaces are declared in the schema DSL … Any name with dot-separated components implicitly declares all intermediate namespaces:" followed at :60-67 by `namespace app.commerce` / `table Order { … }`. railroad.md:69-81 `Statement ::= ImportDecl | TypeDecl | TraitDecl | TableDecl | Binding | RetainDecl | StandaloneAssert | StandaloneUnique | EvolutionStmt | ModeStmt | FunctionDecl | TypeSigDecl` — no `NamespaceDecl`. I read the Reserved Words block at railroad.md:876-893 in full: `namespace` is absent. schema/README.md:70-71 — "Namespaces are created implicitly when a table is first defined in them — no explicit creation syntax." `grep -rn '^namespace '` over docs/ returns exactly one hit: namespaces.md:60.
- **Why it is wrong:** The only worked example in the canonical namespaces document opens with a statement the normative grammar cannot parse, using an unreserved word (so it lexes as an ordinary `Ident` and the line would be read as a stray `FunctionDecl`/expression head). It also contradicts the sentence directly above it and the settled rule in schema/README.md. A second consequence: with no namespace-scoping statement and no file-level current-namespace rule anywhere, the short-name `table Order { … }` at :62 has nothing to resolve `Order` against. The nearest real mechanism is the REPL-only `:use <namespace>` (railroad.md:766, cli.md:62/78), which is not schema-file syntax.
- **Fix:** In docs/namespaces.md#namespace-declarations delete line 60 and write the example fully qualified: `table app.commerce.Order { … }`, `customer :> Customer`. Replace the lead sentence at :57 with "Namespaces are not declared. Any dot-separated name implicitly creates its intermediate namespaces." If a file-level current namespace is genuinely wanted, that is a grammar change: add `NamespaceDecl ::= 'namespace' QName` to `Statement` in railroad.md:69-81, add `namespace` to the Reserved Words block, and specify its extent (to the next `namespace` or end of file) and its precedence in short-name lookup.

### [major] The namespace tree keeps a top-level `reference/` branch annotated with replication behaviour — the namespace/trait conflation the same file corrects 44 lines later

- **Where:** docs/namespaces.md:34, docs/namespaces.md:78, docs/schema/traits.md:101, docs/schema/traits.md:113-118, docs/open-questions.md:394, docs/schema/README.md:76-80
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/namespaces.md
- **Evidence:** namespaces.md:34, inside the namespace tree: "├── reference/           -- reference data shards (propagated everywhere)". namespaces.md:78: "`system` is **not** among those traits: it is a namespace, and a table in it carries whichever replication trait fits. … The namespace says whose a table is and who may see it; the trait says how it propagates." traits.md:101 lists `Reference` as a replication trait. OQ-005:394: "**`system` is a namespace, not a replication class.**"
- **Why it is wrong:** `Reference` is a replication trait. A top-level namespace named after it and annotated "propagated everywhere" is the same category error the file corrects for `system` — it implies replication follows namespace membership. A grep of docs/ finds no table declared in a `reference.*` namespace, so the branch is also orphaned, and it has no counterpart in schema/README.md:76-80, which lists exactly three layers (`connectors.*`, `app.*`, `system.*`), so the two documents disagree on the top level of the tree.
- **Fix:** Delete the `reference/` branch and its blank separator line from the tree at namespaces.md:33-35, leaving the top level as `system/`, `connectors/`, `app/` to match schema/README.md:76-80.

### [major] The namespace tree names system tables in snake_case and lists two tables the event model deleted

- **Where:** docs/namespaces.md:26-32, docs/api.md:41, docs/api.md:69, docs/api.md:190, docs/events.md:505-517, docs/open-questions.md:490-496, docs/schema/README.md:46-53
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED

Actual declarations: api.md:41 `table system.api.GeneratedRoute`, api.md:53 `table system.api.FormatFunctor`, api.md:69 `table system.api.CustomRoute`, api.md:190 `table system.logs.HttpRequest`, events.md:524 `table system.events.QueuePolicy`. events.md:505 removes `system.events.Item`; events.md:511 removes `system.events.Queue`.
- **Why it is wrong:** Every name in the tree violates the mandated `UpperCamelCase` singular table convention (schema/README.md:97), and `queues` and `items` name the two tables the event model explicitly deleted. schema/README.md:46-53 gives the correct names for the same tables, so the repository's two indexes of system state disagree.
- **Fix:** Drop the per-namespace table lists from the tree rather than re-writing them, since a second list guarantees the drift recurs: annotate each branch with its purpose only (`api/ -- route and format registration, see api.md`; `events/ -- scheduler policy and state, see events.md`; `logs/ -- operational logs, see api.md`). If the lists are kept, correct them to `GeneratedRoute, CustomRoute, FormatFunctor` / `QueuePolicy, BackoffState, SchedulerLimit, Handler, HandlerConfig, TriggerState` / `HttpRequest`.

The example also relies on an ambient current namespace so that `table Order` resolves to `app.commerce.Order`, which no document specifies outside the REPL, and the lead-in sentence contradicts itself — namespaces are "declared", then declared "implicitly".

### [major] Name resolution inside a schema file is unspecified: nothing establishes a current namespace, and `ImportDecl`'s `ModuleName` is undefined

- **Where:** docs/namespaces.md:70-72, docs/schema/railroad.md:82, docs/schema/railroad.md:766, docs/cli.md:69, docs/schema/README.md:290
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/README.md
- **Evidence:** namespaces.md:71-72: "Within the same namespace, tables can refer to each other by short name." The only mechanism resembling one is REPL-only: railroad.md:766 `MetaCommand ::= ':use' QName`, and cli.md:69 "The current namespace context is a convenience default for unqualified names." The file-level construct is `ImportDecl ::= 'import' ModuleName ( '(' Ident ( ',' Ident )* ')' )?` (railroad.md:82), and nothing says whether a `ModuleName` is a namespace or how an imported `Ident` resolves against a same-named local one.
- **Why it is wrong:** `TableDecl ::= 'table' QName` admits a bare `Ident`, and the docs use one repeatedly — `table Bar : A, B` (schema/README.md:290), `table Order { … }` (namespaces.md:62), `trait Catalog : Reference` (traits.md:124). None has a defined fully-qualified name, yet the fully-qualified name is load-bearing everywhere: it addresses validations (schema/README.md:265-303), keys `system.shards.ExtentPolicy` rows (OQ-005:393), names the subject of a grant, and is what `:describe` prints. An implementer cannot write the resolver or say whether two files declaring `table Order` collide. OQ-005:409 lists "package import scope" as open, but that is Haskell package imports, not schema name resolution.
- **Fix:** Add a "Name resolution" subsection to schema/README.md's Notation Conventions stating: whether a schema file has a current namespace and how it is set; the shadowing order (local declaration > import > fully-qualified); whether an unqualified `TableDecl` at file scope is an error or resolves to a default; and what `ImportDecl`'s `ModuleName` names. Replace the assertion at namespaces.md:71 with a link to it.

### [major] namespaces.md says shard assignment follows trait and data volume, and asserts a namespace→shard mapping table that does not exist

- **Where:** docs/namespaces.md:76, docs/schema/tables.md:157-176, docs/distribution.md:195-201, docs/transaction-graph.md:158
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/tables.md#keys-must-be-rooted; namespaces.md should link
- **Evidence:** namespaces.md:76 — "the shard assignment is determined by the table's replication trait (`Reference`, `Configuration`, `UserData`, `LogData`, `Component`) and data volume, not by namespace. The mapping between namespaces and shards is maintained in the system tables and is transparent to queries." tables.md:159-162 — "On a shard-local table the key also determines placement … **A candidate key on a `UserData` table must reach the shard root through its foreign-key chain.**" distribution.md:195-197 — "The partition function ranges over **shard root rows**, and the key it partitions on is the root table's candidate key — which is why that key is mandatory". distribution.md:222-224 places volume as the trigger for a *split*, requiring `split shard … at key`. transaction-graph.md:158 — "A shard is rooted at a **row**, not at a table."
- **Why it is wrong:** The trait selects the replication family; within `UserData` the concrete shard is chosen per row by the key's FK chain to a shard root. Volume triggers a split, it does not assign. And because shards are row-rooted there is no stored namespace→shard mapping — placement is computed from the key. As written the paragraph reproduces the pre-row-rooted model and sends an implementer looking for a system table that does not exist.
- **Fix:** Replace docs/namespaces.md:76 with: "Namespaces are a logical organization; shards are a physical one, and a namespace does not map to a shard. The replication trait selects the shard family. Within a shard-local family, a row's shard is the row-rooted shard reached by its table's candidate key through the foreign-key chain — see [schema/tables.md](schema/tables.md#keys-must-be-rooted). Data volume triggers a split, not an assignment." Delete the "mapping … maintained in the system tables" sentence.

### [major] A table declared with no trait list has no defined replication trait, and that is the commonest form in the examples

- **Where:** docs/namespaces.md:62, docs/schema/railroad.md:196, docs/schema/traits.md:94-97, docs/transaction-graph.md:109-110, docs/schema/README.md:237, docs/schema/constraints.md:63
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED

'{' TableBody '}'`. traits.md:96-97 — "Tables declare their replication policy by extending one of these." transaction-graph.md:109-110 — "Four shard types, each corresponding to a built-in replication trait". Trait-less declarations appear at namespaces.md:62, schema/README.md:237, schema/constraints.md:63 and elsewhere. `grep -rn 'default.*replication trait|UserData.*by default'` over docs/ returns only queries.md:308, which is about bindings inheriting from sources.
- **Why it is wrong:** Every table must land in some shard and the shard follows the trait, but no document states a default for an omitted trait list. The consequence is not cosmetic: under `UserData` the key-rooting rule at tables.md:161 applies and constrains whether `unique orderRef { customer, order_num }` is even legal; under `Reference` or `Configuration` it does not.

Pick one and confirm the trait-less examples still satisfy the key rule.

### [major] Name resolution — short names, the current namespace, and ambiguity — is specified nowhere

- **Where:** docs/namespaces.md:5, docs/namespaces.md:70-72, docs/schema/railroad.md:82, docs/schema/functions.md:161, docs/open-questions.md:409
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/namespaces.md
- **Evidence:** namespaces.md:71-72 — "Within the same namespace, tables can refer to each other by short name." That is the only statement of a resolution rule in the corpus. No document says how a schema file establishes its current namespace (the `namespace` statement at :60 is not in the grammar — see the blocker above), what happens when a short name is ambiguous, or whether a name resolves upward through ancestor namespaces. evolution.md#how-a-commit-resolves-names covers only *version* resolution.
- **Why it is wrong:** Without a current-namespace rule, "tables can refer to each other by short name" has no operational meaning in a schema file, and every short-name example in the documents — `table Order { customer :> Customer }`, `ActiveOrder = Order where …` — is unresolvable. The Python analogy at namespaces.md:5 actively misleads: Python has no implicit same-package short names.
- **Fix:** Add a "Name resolution" section to docs/namespaces.md giving the lookup order (local `let` binding → current namespace → explicit imports → fully qualified), the current-namespace rule for a schema file, and the ambiguity rule (a compile-time error naming both candidates, never shadowing — consistent with railroad.md:906-908). Drop or qualify the Python analogy. Note separately that `ImportDecl` (railroad.md:82) is a *Haskell package* import per functions.md:161, whose scope open-questions.md:409 already tracks as open — say so in the new section so a reader does not read it as a namespace import.
- **Verifier note:** The candidate claimed no document says what `import` does; that is partly refuted — functions.md:161 scopes it to Haskell packages and OQ-005 lists its scope as open. The narrowed finding is namespace name resolution.

### [major] "The system shard" is working vocabulary in ten files, but `system` was explicitly withdrawn as a shard type and the term is defined nowhere

- **Where:** docs/namespaces.md:16, docs/transaction-graph.md:123-125, docs/transaction-graph.md:146-148, docs/schema/traits.md:113-118, docs/schema/traits.md:330, docs/schema/constraints.md:189, docs/auth.md:478, docs/auth.md:542-543, docs/integrity.md:250, docs/cli.md:357, docs/ide.md:7
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED

Against that, `grep -rn 'system shard|`system` shard'` over docs/ returns eleven hits, including namespaces.md:16 "Stored as nodes in the system shard", traits.md:330 "committed to the schema graph in the `system` shard", auth.md:478, constraints.md:189, integrity.md:250, cli.md:357, ide.md:7.

Where schema nodes are meant, write "the schema shard (one per branch)" and link [transaction-graph.md](transaction-graph.md#data-shards) — namespaces.md:16, traits.md:330, integrity.md:250. Where "replicated to every server" is meant, name the trait — constraints.md:189, auth.md:478/542. Add a one-line note under transaction-graph.md#data-shards that "system shard" is not a term of the model.

### [major] The namespace tree advertises `system.events.Queue` and `system.events.Item`, both explicitly removed

- **Where:** docs/namespaces.md:28, docs/events.md:504-509, docs/events.md:511-515, docs/schema/traits.md:373-374
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/events.md#system-tables
- **Evidence:** namespaces.md:28 — "│   ├── events/          -- queues, items, backoff_state, maintenance_queue". events.md:504 — "**`system.events.Item` is gone.** It carried `payload : Bytes`, which duplicated the queue row". events.md:511 — "**`system.events.Queue` is gone.** A queue's existence and its handler binding are *already* schema facts". traits.md:373 — "`system.events.Queue` was specified and then removed on this rule". ### [major] Visibility is called "purely a presentation hint" while the same table and schema/README.md treat it as authorization

- **Where:** docs/namespaces.md:103-113, docs/namespaces.md:107, docs/schema/README.md:79, docs/namespaces.md:119-124
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/namespaces.md#schema-visibility-layers
- **Evidence:** namespaces.md:113 — "Visibility is stored as a field on the schema transaction graph node. It can be changed without affecting the underlying data or query behavior — it is purely a presentation hint for the IDE and schema PageRank calculation." The same table at namespaces.md:107 — "| `system` | DataCode internals | No (admin override only) |". schema/README.md:79 — "**System schemas** (`system.*`): DataCode internals; visible only to admin tokens". The settled reachability model is namespaces.md:119-124 — "default-deny with recursive grants (OQ-024)".
- **Why it is wrong:** "Admin override only" and "visible only to admin tokens" are access-control statements; "purely a presentation hint … without affecting query behavior" says the opposite. Under OQ-024 reachability is decided by grants, not by a visibility level, so schema/README.md:79 asserts a second, competing authorization mechanism. An implementer cannot tell whether the visibility field is consulted on a query path.
- **Fix:** Keep visibility strictly presentational. In docs/namespaces.md#schema-visibility-layers change the `system` row's column to "No (IDE default; reachability is a separate grant)". Change docs/schema/README.md:79 to "**System schemas** (`system.*`): DataCode internals; reachable only with a grant on `system`, and hidden in the default IDE view."

### [major] `bypass access` semantics are stated normatively in four files, in four wordings, cross-linked in a cycle

- **Where:** docs/namespaces.md:138-140, docs/auth.md:458-460, docs/schema/constraints.md:262-264, docs/cli.md:179-181
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/namespaces.md#bypass
- **Evidence:** namespaces.md:138-140 — "`bypass access` skips every `assert` that mentions `authed_user`, **on read and on write**, and **skips nothing else**. Data constraints still run: an administrator is exempt from access control, never from data integrity." auth.md:458-460 — "Every assert mentioning `authed_user` is skipped for a token holding that grant; every other assert still runs. **An administrator is exempt from access control, never from data integrity.**" constraints.md:262-264 — near-identical. cli.md:179-181 — "exempts the grant from every `assert` that mentions `authed_user` and from nothing else — data constraints still run." Links: namespaces.md:158 → cli.md#grants and auth.md#schema-level-access-and-bypass; constraints.md:266-267 → auth.md and namespaces.md; cli.md:182 → namespaces.md#bypass. No file is designated authoritative.
- **Why it is wrong:** Four normative statements of one security rule, and the drift has already started: only namespaces.md carries "on read and on write", so the other three leave open whether a bypass applies to reads. This is the defect the project's one-normative-home rule names, on the rule a reader can least afford to guess about.
- **Fix:** Name docs/namespaces.md#bypass the home — cli.md and constraints.md already link there. Reduce auth.md:458-462, constraints.md:262-264 and cli.md:179-181 to one sentence each ("A `bypass access` grant is exempt from row-level access asserts and from nothing else; see [namespaces.md](namespaces.md#bypass)") with no restatement of the boundary. Keep the CLI spelling in cli.md, which is its own home.
- **Verifier note:** The candidate's sub-claim that auth.md:445 and constraints.md:248 sharing the heading "Schema-Level Access and Bypass" makes the anchors indistinguishable is dropped — cross-file links always carry the filename.

### [major] A top-level `reference/` namespace survives in the namespace tree, the same defect that was corrected for `system`

- **Why it is wrong:** `reference/` in the tree is a namespace whose stated content is "reference data shards (propagated everywhere)" — i.e. a namespace defined by its replication policy, which is precisely the conflation the `system` correction removed. `Reference` is a trait; a `Reference` table can live in `app.commerce` or `system.crypto` (both do), so the tree implies a rule the design rejects.
- **Fix:** Delete the `reference/` node from namespaces.md:34, or relabel it as an ordinary application namespace with no replication meaning, and add the one-line reminder that replication is a trait.

### [minor] "DataId primary key is implicit" versus "no implicit keys unless declared"

Both are reconcilable under the project invariant — `DataId` is an implicit row *identifier*, not a candidate key (tables.md:132-134 makes exactly that distinction) — but no document says so, and "primary key" is relational vocabulary the rest of the language avoids in favour of "candidate key".

### [minor] A top-level `reference/` namespace "for reference data shards" conflates namespace with replication class

- **Where:** docs/namespaces.md:34, docs/namespaces.md:76-78, docs/schema/traits.md:113-118
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/namespaces.md
- **Evidence:** namespaces.md:34 — "├── reference/           -- reference data shards (propagated everywhere)". namespaces.md:76 — "Namespaces are a logical organization; shards are a physical one." namespaces.md:78 — "`system` is **not** among those traits: it is a namespace, and a table in it carries whichever replication trait fits." `grep -rn '\breference\.[a-zA-Z]'` over docs/ returns nothing — no `reference.*` qualified name exists anywhere, and every `Reference` table named in the documents lives under `system.*` or `app.*` (`system.crypto.HashPolicy`, `app.commerce.OrderStatus`, `app.ui.Template`).
- **Why it is wrong:** The tree defines a namespace whose stated purpose is to be a shard class — the precise conflation the same file rules out for `system` forty lines later, and that traits.md and transaction-graph.md both correct. Replication is decided by the `Reference` trait, which any table in any namespace may carry, so there is nothing for a `reference` namespace to mean.
- **Fix:** Delete the `reference/` branch from the docs/namespaces.md:22-53 tree. If grouping shared code tables under one namespace is wanted, describe it by ownership ("shared code tables maintained centrally") rather than by replication, and cite a table that lives there.

### [minor] How an external table name becomes a DataCode name in a connector shadow schema is unspecified, and both spellings appear

- **Where:** docs/namespaces.md:39-46, docs/namespaces.md:84, docs/namespaces.md:92, docs/connectors.md:169, docs/schema/railroad.md:796, docs/open-questions.md:968-972
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/namespaces.md#connector-namespaces

OQ-025 (open-questions.md:968-972) covers propagation of schema *changes*, not naming.
- **Why it is wrong:** Both spellings appear for the same table in one file and no rule says which is produced. An implementer needs the algorithm: does `orders` become `Order`? What about `order_items`, `ORDERS`, `2020_orders` (not a valid `Ident`), or a source carrying both `order` and `orders`? The connector *instance* name also becomes a namespace segment via `add connector Ident …` (railroad.md:796), where `Ident` admits uppercase while the convention requires lowercase segments.
- **Fix:** Add a naming rule to docs/namespaces.md#connector-namespaces (or connectors.md, with a link from there): source identifiers are transliterated to `UpperCamelCase` singular; a name that collides with an existing table, or that cannot form an `Ident`, is recorded as a violation and the table is skipped until an override row names it. Constrain the connector instance `Ident` at railroad.md:796 to lowercase.

### [minor] A recursive grant silently reaches namespaces and tables created after it

- **Where:** docs/namespaces.md:119-124, docs/open-questions.md:940-954
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/namespaces.md#namespace-access-control
- **Evidence:** namespaces.md:122 — "A client token granted access to `app.commerce` automatically has access to all tables in that namespace and its children". namespaces.md:124 — "Grants are per-subtree and explicit: a grant on `app` reaches only `app` and its descendants." OQ-024 — "**Grants recurse to children.** A grant on a namespace reaches that namespace and every descendant namespace, table, view, and functor within it." Neither says the subtree is mutable.
- **Why it is wrong:** The schema is data and the subtree evolves, so creating `app.hr.Salary` under an existing grant on `app` grants access to it at the moment of the schema commit, with no second decision by anyone. That is a defensible design, but it is a security property neither namespaces.md nor OQ-024 states, and an implementer cannot tell whether to warn at commit, require a re-grant, or do nothing.
- **Fix:** Add to docs/namespaces.md#namespace-access-control: "A grant is over the subtree as it evolves, not as it stood when the grant was written — a table created under a granted namespace is reachable by that grant from its commit." State whether creating a table under a `bypass`-bearing grant warns at commit. Add the same as a bullet under OQ-024.

### [minor] "Each coercion is a named function" but the example's first coercion is a bare arithmetic expression

### [minor] "Old paths remain valid" is stated three different ways in one file, and none matches evolution.md

- **Where:** docs/namespaces.md:18, docs/namespaces.md:163, docs/namespaces.md:165, docs/schema/evolution.md:171-179
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED

Deprecate the old one when ready."
- **Why it is wrong:** The three sentences say three different things: valid at head; resolvable only with an `at` clause; and working only if the client adds a pin — which is exactly what a hard-coded path cannot do. evolution.md gives a fourth, concrete mechanism (both names live at head until `deprecate`), which is the one that actually supports :18.

What remains is `QueuePolicy`, `BackoffState`, and `SchedulerLimit`, all `Configuration`."

### [minor] namespaces.md lists a removed system table and puts branches and tags in a different namespace from every other document

- **Where:** docs/namespaces.md:28, docs/namespaces.md:30, docs/events.md:504, docs/transaction-graph.md:50, docs/transaction-graph.md:65, docs/schema/README.md:51

- **Why it is wrong:** The namespace tree is where a reader looks up where a system table lives. It advertises `items` — deleted, not renamed — and puts branches and tags under `system.schema` while three other documents put them at `system.VersionRef`. `system.events.Queue` (also removed) is arguably still implied by "queues" too.

### [nit] "Data independence" names two different properties in two files

- **Where:** docs/namespaces.md:167, docs/schema/README.md:81-83
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/README.md (the term)
- **Evidence:** namespaces.md:167 — "This is a core property of the data independence model: the physical and historical structure is never destroyed, only the active view changes." schema/README.md:81-83 — "This layering enables data independence: the human-understood schema (`app.*`) can evolve independently of the physical/connector schema underneath it, with coercion handled by functors between the layers."
- **Why it is wrong:** Data independence in the ANSI/SPARC sense is the insulation of an application from changes at the layer below it. Never destroying history and keeping old graph nodes queryable is schema versioning and temporal query — a different property; a system can have perfect version history and no data independence, and the reverse. schema/README.md uses the term correctly, so namespaces.md gives the same phrase a second meaning.
- **Fix:** docs/namespaces.md:167 → "This is a consequence of the append-only schema graph: no structure is destroyed, so every historical name stays resolvable." Reserve "data independence" for the layering claim in schema/README.md.
