The pointer sends a reader to a decision record that says the opposite of the sentence citing it.
- **Fix:** Replace category-model.md:62 with "- Written `on <condition> emit <queue> { … }` or `every <interval> emit <queue> { … } where <condition>` on the producing table, with `handler` on the queue (OQ-030). See [schema/functors.md](schema/functors.md#event-functor) and [events.md](events.md)."

### [major] Static "consistency and completeness" analysis of access rules is claimed in four places with no fragment, no algorithm, and no definition of a gap

- **Where:** docs/category-model.md:53, docs/schema/functors.md:144, docs/schema/functors.md:198, docs/auth.md:419, docs/schema/constraints.md:89, docs/vision.md:15
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/category-model.md
- **Evidence:** category-model.md:53: "access rules can be statically analyzed for consistency (no contradictions, no gaps) before deployment by exactly the analysis that checks data constraints". functors.md:144: "access rules can be checked statically for consistency and completeness the same way data constraints can". auth.md:419: "Access rules can be analyzed statically for consistency (no contradictions, complete …". constraints.md:89: "This also keeps the static completeness analysis tractable".
- **Why it is wrong:** Asserts admit conjunctive queries (presence, constraints.md:177-183) and their negations (absence), conjoined across a table, and nothing in docs/ restricts the fragment. Containment for conjunctive queries is NP-complete and the implication problem for embedded dependencies is undecidable in general, so an unqualified "can be statically analyzed for consistency before deployment" is at best an incomplete procedure described as a total one. "No gaps" is worse than hard, it is undefined: OQ-024:945-948 settles the model as default-deny with recursive grants, in which an ungranted row is the normal case, so "gap" cannot mean "a row no rule reaches" and no document says what it does mean.
- **Fix:** State the fragment and the guarantee once, in category-model.md's access-constraint section, and link the other three sites to it: for asserts restricted to anchored single-valued paths without negation, unsatisfiability is decidable by congruence closure over the declared path equations; with negation the checker is sound but incomplete and must report "cannot decide" rather than "consistent". Delete "no gaps" from category-model.md:53, "and completeness" from functors.md:144, "complete" from auth.md:419, and "completeness" from constraints.md:89 — or define what a gap is under default-deny before claiming to detect one.

### [major] The revalidation set is called finite and bounded by anchoring; backward FK traversal has no bound, no algorithm, and no exclusion rule

- **Where:** docs/category-model.md:143, docs/schema/functors.md:62-64, docs/schema/constraints.md:193-196, docs/open-questions.md:144, docs/open-questions.md:373
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/constraints.md
- **Evidence:** category-model.md:143: "the same rootedness restriction is what makes 'the affected subgraph' finite and findable, by traversing the declared morphisms backwards from the written row." functors.md:62: "Anchoring is what makes 'the affected subgraph' a finite thing to name". constraints.md:193-196 is more careful: "**It does not make absence cheap to maintain.** … Anchoring is what makes that set findable: it is the FK chain, traversed backwards. Without it there would be no bound at all."
- **Why it is wrong:** Traversing a foreign key backwards is a preimage and its size is unbounded: writing one `Reference` row reaches every row in the cluster that references it and, transitively, the whole connected component. "Findable" is true; "finite" is vacuous (the database is finite) and reads as "small", which is what an implementer will build against. OQ-005:373 already excludes FKs into `Reference`/`Configuration` from *key rooting* for this reason, but no rule excludes them from *backward revalidation*, and OQ-027:144 confirms the set can cross shards. No algorithm, no bound, and no statement of behaviour when the set is large.
- **Fix:** In schema/constraints.md#anchoring (the normative home) add the revalidation-set rule: the set is the backward closure over declared `:>` edges from the written row restricted to edges appearing in some assert's path; state explicitly whether edges into `Reference` and `Configuration` tables participate; and state the behaviour when the set exceeds a threshold (reject the write, or coerce the attachment to `monitor`, as OQ-027:144 already does for shard-crossing asserts). Change category-model.md:143 and functors.md:62 to "findable" and drop "finite".

### [major] The closed-form behavior class is presented as a settled property of the model; OQ-034 records the class, the solver and the encoding as all open

- **Where:** docs/category-model.md:116-126, docs/open-questions.md:598-640, docs/schema/functors.md:165-168, docs/events.md:581-591
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/open-questions.md (OQ-034)
- **Evidence:** category-model.md:117-121 says "when does this become true?" has "been answerable only by polling" and that a behavior "has a solution rather than a search, and the event scheduler can ask it directly"; :123-126: "The restriction to a closed-form-solvable class of behaviors follows from the same place… The class is a constraint on the *category*, not a performance concession: it is what keeps 'when does this condition first hold?' a morphism rather than a procedure." OQ-034:606-608: "The class, the solver per class, and the encoding of both in the GADT DSL are unspecified." OQ-034:631-635: "`every` unblocks the use case without answering the question… sampling is exactly the polling solving exists to eliminate."
- **Why it is wrong:** The foundation document asserts the restriction as established and never mentions `every` or OQ-034, while OQ-034 records the analyzable class as undefined, the solver as unbuilt, re-solving on write as undecided, and missed-crossing policy as undecided — and records that the shipped path today is sampling, i.e. the polling lines 117-121 present as eliminated. A reader of category-model.md alone concludes behaviors can trigger events today; functors.md:167 and events.md:581 say otherwise. Separately, "a morphism rather than a procedure" is not a claim the design supports: a crossing solver returns a `Moment`, and there is no object in the schema category for it to be an arrow into.
- **Fix:** Append to category-model.md:126: "The class itself, the per-class solver, and their encoding in the DSL are open — see OQ-034. Until they land, an open-form behavior is sampled with `every`, which is polling with bounded lateness." Delete the clause "it is what keeps 'when does this condition first hold?' a morphism rather than a procedure".

### [major] The denotative claim is made for the whole language but supplied only for `Behavior`, and the query peg is stated with one parameter where the rest of the design uses two

- **Where:** docs/category-model.md:97-99, docs/category-model.md:108, docs/category-model.md:111-113, docs/open-questions.md:827-828, docs/storage.md:200-202, docs/schema/functors.md:23-26
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/category-model.md
- **Evidence:** category-model.md:97-99: "DataCode is a **denotative, continuous-time** system in Conal Elliott's sense: every construct has a meaning as a mathematical function, independent of how it is evaluated". Line 108: "Views are queries pegged to a commit node". Line 111-112: "`Behavior a ≅ Moment -> a` is what a query's `at` clause has always computed". OQ-012:827-828: "A query is pegged to a `(commit node, sample moment)` pair"; storage.md:200-202 agrees. functors.md:23-25: the handler "runs in `Effect`, outside the commit, and is compiled-in Haskell rather than a DSL term. That is why it can be arbitrary Haskell when functors cannot".
- **Why it is wrong:** Two problems in one section. (1) The claim is unqualified and false of `Effect`: OQ-030:474-476 records that handlers are "not inspected by the optimizer, not part of static access analysis, and never replayed", so "every construct" invites the reader to expect solvability and replayability the design denies. The accurate and stronger claim is the one the table below already makes — the discipline holds inside the effect ladder up to `Tx`, and the missing lift is what keeps the non-denotative part outside. (2) Denotations are given for exactly two constructs, and the one place a query's denotation is touched is inconsistent: line 108 pegs a view to a commit node while line 113 pegs it to a moment, where OQ-012 and storage.md peg it to both. Under `Moment -> a` alone a query over a schema-evolved table has no well-defined meaning, since which fields exist is a function of the graph point, not the moment.
- **Fix:** Qualify category-model.md:97-99: "Every construct inside the effect ladder — `Pure`, `Read`, `Tx` — has a meaning as a mathematical function, independent of how it is evaluated. Handlers run in `Effect` and are deliberately outside this discipline; the missing lift is what keeps them out." Change line 108 to "Views are queries pegged to a `(commit node, sample moment)` pair" and add after line 113: "A query therefore denotes `(CommitNode, Moment) -> Table`, with `Behavior a ≅ Moment -> a` the special case at a fixed node."

### [major] "The runtime is the governing monad" names no monad and cannot express the missing lift the design turns on

- **Where:** docs/category-model.md:5-12, docs/category-model.md:106, docs/schema/functions.md:30-48, docs/open-questions.md:18-22
- **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/functions.md
- **Evidence:** category-model.md:5: "The DataCode **runtime is the governing monad**. Every operation that reads or writes data, validates a type, traverses a relationship, or checks authorization is a computation within this monad." functions.md:42-48: "`Pure ⊂ Read ⊂ Tx` — each lifts into the next… `Effect` sits outside that chain and connects to it through exactly one arrow: `commit :: Tx a -> Effect a` … `Effect a -> Tx a` does not, and will not". OQ-001:19-20: "`data Eff = Pure | Read | Tx` has **no `Effect` rung**".
- **Why it is wrong:** No endofunctor, unit, bind or law is given, so the claim is unimplementable as written, and the same document already knows better at line 106 ("No lift from `Effect` into `Tx`"). It is also the wrong structure: the load-bearing property is that one lift is *missing*, and within a single monad every computation composes with every other. What is described is a graded (effect-indexed) monad over `Pure ≤ Read ≤ Tx` plus a separate `Effect` monad with a one-way morphism. The four things lines 7-10 say the monad "encapsulates" (schema point, auth context, shard topology, evaluation environment) are a Reader environment and need no monad at all.
- **Fix:** Replace category-model.md:5 with: "DataCode's runtime is a **graded monad** indexed by the effect lattice `Pure ≤ Read ≤ Tx`, together with a separate `Effect` monad and a one-way morphism `commit :: Tx a -> Effect a`. Every operation that reads or writes data, validates a type, traverses a relationship, or checks authorization is a computation at one of those grades." Replace lines 7-10 with a link to [schema/functions.md](schema/functions.md#the-effect-ladder) plus one sentence naming the ambient context (schema point, tokens, topology) as the reader environment each grade carries.
- **Verifier note:** The prose is loose rather than flatly contradictory — "the governing monad" could be read as informal. Confirmed that no monad is defined anywhere in docs/ and that the settled structure is four effects with one missing lift, which a single monad cannot present.

### [major] Path-equation entailment is assumed available to the optimizer with no restriction on the equation set anywhere in docs/

- **Where:** docs/category-model.md:134-139, docs/category-model.md:150, docs/schema/functors.md:196-198
- **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE
- **Normative home:** docs/category-model.md
- **Evidence:** category-model.md:134-137: "A schema is a **finitely presented category** where: Objects = tables (or types) / Morphisms = foreign keys and functional dependencies / Equations = commutative diagram constraints (path equivalences)". category-model.md:150: "Query optimization: the optimizer can reorder functor application when commutativity can be proven". functors.md:196-198 repeats the transparency-enables-analysis claim.
- **Why it is wrong:** Deciding whether a finite presentation of a category entails an equation between two paths is the word problem for categories, undecidable in general (a one-object category is a monoid). The standard treatment — FQL/CQL — requires the declared equation set to be a convergent rewriting system obtained by Knuth–Bendix completion and fails loudly when completion does not terminate. DataCode declares itself finitely presented and leaves the equation set unrestricted, with no OQ tracking it. Note that instance-level checking (evaluate two single-valued paths on one row and compare) is decidable and cheap and is what the mutation path at line 143 actually describes — a different operation from what line 150 needs.
- **Fix:** In category-model.md's "Path Equivalence" section, distinguish the two operations explicitly: instance-level constraint checking (decidable, per row, what mutation validation does) versus schema-level entailment (what the optimizer needs, decidable only for a convergent presentation). State the restriction — declared path equations must form a convergent rewriting system, checked at schema commit, with non-termination a commit error naming the offending pair — and open an OQ for the completion bound and the diagnostic. Cite Spivak & Wisnesky, *Algebraic Databases*.
- **Verifier note:** Line 150 hedges with "when commutativity can be proven", so this is an unaddressed gap rather than a false claim. Confirmed by grep that no document mentions confluence, termination, completion, or any restriction on the equation set, and no OQ covers it.

### [minor] category-model.md restates three rules whose homes are elsewhere, and all three copies have drifted

- **Where:** docs/category-model.md:162, docs/category-model.md:152, docs/category-model.md:75-76, docs/schema/types.md:314-326, docs/schema/functions.md:30-32, docs/schema/functions.md:50-54, docs/open-questions.md:400, docs/integrity.md:202-212, docs/integrity.md:226
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/types.md, docs/schema/functions.md, docs/integrity.md
- **Evidence:** (a) category-model.md:162: "Built-in members are `NotFound`, `Redacted`, `Pending`, and `Deleted`" — types.md:314-326 lists nine, adding `Erased`, `Sealed`, `JsonNull`, `NoKey`, `NotRetained`. (b) category-model.md:152: "Opaque functions (arbitrary IO, FFI calls with side effects) are not permitted inside functors" — OQ-005:400: "This **replaces the `a -> IO b` signature rejection**, which was weaker … `IO` no longer appears in any DataCode signature at all", and functions.md:31-32 says the same. (c) category-model.md:75-76: "a **violation** is a row that records the triple `(subject, violated functor, schema node)`" — integrity.md:202-212 declares seven fields and integrity.md:226 states "The pair `(subject_table, subject)` *is* the existential, written out by hand."
- **Why it is wrong:** Each is a second normative statement of a rule with a home elsewhere, and each copy is now wrong in a way that matters. (a) omits `Erased` and `Sealed`, the two variants a read can produce without them appearing in any declaration. (b) states the weaker mechanism that was explicitly withdrawn and names a type the language does not have; in the file that exists to explain *why*, the structural reason (a missing lift, not a prohibition) is the interesting one and is the one omitted. (c) drops `subject_table`, which integrity.md:215-227 spends a subsection explaining is required because a bare `DataId` cannot resolve without a named target table — the design point the summary erases.
- **Fix:** Three edits in one pass. (a) category-model.md:162 → "Built-in members cover the recurring reasons — not found, redacted, sealed, erased, not retained; the full list is in [schema/types.md](schema/types.md#absence-types). Schema authors add their own." Keep the `Maybe` contrast, which is the *why* and belongs here. (b) category-model.md:152 → "Opaque computation is not merely disallowed inside a functor, it is unrepresentable: `Effect` has no lift into `Tx`, so there is no type an external call could produce there. See [schema/functions.md](schema/functions.md#the-effect-ladder)." (c) category-model.md:75-76 → "a **violation** is a row recording `(subject_table, subject)`, the violated functor, and the schema node — see [integrity.md](integrity.md#the-violations-table) for the full row and why the subject is an explicit pair."

### [minor] The anchoring rule in category-model.md drops "in either direction", which is what makes a presence assertion non-vacuous

- **Where:** docs/category-model.md:141, docs/category-model.md:40, docs/schema/constraints.md:177-178, docs/schema/railroad.md:253-254, docs/open-questions.md:362
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/constraints.md
- **Evidence:** category-model.md:141: "**Presence** asserts that the set of rows reached by a composition is inhabited … the composition must start at the row under evaluation and every step must be a declared morphism." constraints.md:177-178: "An assert's query must be rooted at `self`, and every subsequent source must be reached by a join along a declared `:>` edge **in either direction**." railroad.md:253-254 and OQ-005:362 say the same, and OQ-005:362 adds "It also makes the *reverse* direction findable, which is what an absence assertion needs".
- **Why it is wrong:** The same paragraph that justifies presence by single-valuedness (category-model.md:40, "every path in the schema graph is single-valued by construction") then states an anchoring rule permitting only forward steps, along which a presence assertion is trivially satisfied. The set a presence assert quantifies over is a fibre, reached by traversing a `:>` edge backwards — which is also what makes the revalidation set at line 143 findable. Dropping the direction clause removes the only thing that makes the shape meaningful.
- **Fix:** Extend category-model.md:141 to "…every step must be a declared morphism, followed in either direction — forwards to a referent or backwards to its referrers. The backward direction is what a presence or absence assertion quantifies over, since a forward path is single-valued and total. See [schema/constraints.md](schema/constraints.md#anchoring)."
- **Verifier note:** The omission is verbatim-confirmable. The candidate's further claim that the pullback framing at line 40 is backwards (presence is non-emptiness of a fibre, not of a pullback of two paths out of `self`) is sound but is a rewrite of a rationale rather than a contradiction — worth folding into the same edit, not worth a separate finding.

### [minor] A foreign-key chain is called functor composition in the same bullet that calls foreign keys the arrows of the schema category

- **Where:** docs/category-model.md:29-30, docs/category-model.md:136, docs/schema/functors.md:15, docs/vision.md:15
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/category-model.md
- **Evidence:** category-model.md:29-30, under "Foreign Key Functors": "- Encode the \"arrows\" of the schema category / - Compose: a foreign key chain is functor composition". category-model.md:136: "Morphisms = foreign keys and functional dependencies". functors.md:15 gives the FK signature as `DataId → Either Error Row`. vision.md:15: authorization "is a **category of functors** applied to the same schema graph".
- **Why it is wrong:** Arrows compose as morphisms, not as functors — the two clauses of the same bullet contradict each other, and line 136 sides with the first. Given the signature `DataId → Either Error Row`, the composition is Kleisli composition in `Either Error`. "A category of functors" (vision.md:15) names the functor category [C,D], which is not what access rules form.
- **Fix:** Change category-model.md:30 to "- Compose: a foreign key chain is morphism composition — in the implementation, Kleisli composition in `Either Error`". Change vision.md:15 to "it is expressed with the same functors, over the same schema graph, as data relationships". If "functor" is to stay DataCode's term of art for the four attachable rule kinds — and it should, the churn is not worth it — say so once in category-model.md:16 and note that the constructions that are functors in the categorical sense are the instance functor and the migration functors.

### [minor] category-model.md calls composing foreign keys "functor composition" and makes functional dependencies morphisms, contradicting its own presentation two paragraphs later

- **Where:** docs/category-model.md:16, docs/category-model.md:30-31, docs/category-model.md:134-139
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Evidence:** category-model.md:16 — "A functor in DataCode is a structure-preserving mapping between categories. In practice, each functor is a Haskell function applied to a type or relationship that enforces a rule." category-model.md:30-31 (FK functors) — "Encode the 'arrows' of the schema category / **Compose: a foreign key chain is functor composition**". category-model.md:136 — "Morphisms = foreign keys and functional dependencies". category-model.md:139 — "for two paths `f ∘ g` and `h ∘ k` … **the composed functors** must produce the same result. This is **the categorical analog of a referential integrity constraint**".
- **Why it is wrong:** Line 136 correctly makes foreign keys *morphisms*; lines 31 and 139 then call composing them "functor composition". A chain of morphisms composes as morphisms — in Spivak's model the functors are the instance functor `I : C → Set` and a schema morphism `F : C → D`. Line 16's own two sentences contradict each other: a Haskell function `a -> Either Error a` is not a mapping between categories. And a path equation is not "the categorical analog of a referential integrity constraint" — referential integrity is the totality of the FK morphism itself; a path equation is a different and more general thing. Since CLAUDE.md names "four functor kinds" as load-bearing, the terminology is entrenched, which is why the theory page should say plainly that "functor" is DataCode's term of art.
- **Fix:** In docs/category-model.md#functors add one sentence after line 16: "DataCode uses *functor* as its term for a schema-attached rule. ### [minor] Path equivalence is called the categorical analog of referential integrity; RI is the totality the functorial model already gives for free

- **Where:** docs/category-model.md:139, docs/category-model.md:141, docs/category-model.md:27-32
- **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE
- **Normative home:** docs/category-model.md
- **Evidence:** category-model.md:139: "A path equivalence asserts: for two paths `f ∘ g` and `h ∘ k` through the schema graph, the composed functors must produce the same result. This is the categorical analog of a referential integrity constraint, but far more general."
- **Why it is wrong:** Referential integrity is the totality of the foreign-key function; in the functorial model I(f) is total by construction, which is why category-model.md:27-32 lists foreign keys as a separate kind that *resolves* rather than asserts. A path equation is not a generalization of it. In classical dependency theory the three assert shapes have standard names — a path equation is an equality-generating dependency, a presence assert a tuple-generating dependency, an absence assert a denial constraint — and naming them connects the design to the chase, to chase-and-backchase rewriting under constraints, and to the known complexity results, none of which the design currently cites but all of which the optimizer work will need.
- **Fix:** In category-model.md:139 replace "This is the categorical analog of a referential integrity constraint, but far more general" with "This is an equality-generating dependency; referential integrity is instead the totality of the foreign-key map, which the functorial model gives for free." Add one sentence after line 141 classifying the three shapes as equality-generating, tuple-generating, and denial constraints, and naming the chase as the intended evaluation and rewriting machinery.

### [minor] `Event a ≅ [(Time, a)]` is asserted as the storage format; the transaction graph is a branching DAG and timestamps are clamped

- **Where:** docs/category-model.md:107, docs/transaction-graph.md:10, docs/transaction-graph.md:417-425, docs/open-questions.md:399
- **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE
- **Normative home:** docs/category-model.md
- **Evidence:** category-model.md:107: "| Append-only, no in-place update, idempotent records | A row's history *is* `Event a ≅ [(Time, a)]`. Not an analogy; it is the storage format. |" transaction-graph.md:10 describes "an **immutable, append-only directed acyclic graph** (a git-like commit DAG)" with branches, tags and merges; transaction-graph.md:417-424 has a "Clock Regression" section where "the timestamp is held at the last emitted value"; OQ-005:399 records the sequence counter as "a tiebreak rather than an ordering — two servers' values are incomparable".
- **Why it is wrong:** An FRP `Event` is a stream of occurrences totally ordered by one continuous time. A row's history is totally ordered only relative to a branch: with branches and merges the version chain is a tree, and there is no single list. Timestamps are also not strictly increasing across the clamp, and cross-server occurrences within a millisecond are incomparable. Both matter to anything consuming the claim, such as sampling a behavior at a moment across a merge.
- **Fix:** Change the right-hand cell at category-model.md:107 to "Along one branch, a row's history denotes an `Event a ≅ [(Time, a)]`; across branches it is a tree, and a query resolves the branch before the moment." Drop "Not an analogy; it is the storage format."

### [minor] category-model.md defines a functor as a mapping between categories, then describes all four kinds as things that are not

- **Where:** docs/category-model.md:16, docs/category-model.md:29, docs/category-model.md:36, docs/schema/functors.md:12
- **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE
- **Normative home:** docs/category-model.md (Functors)
- **Evidence:** category-model.md:16 "A functor in DataCode is a structure-preserving mapping between categories. In practice, each functor is a Haskell function applied to a type or relationship that enforces a rule." category-model.md:29-30 then says foreign key functors "Encode the **arrows** of the schema category", and :36 cites Spivak's *Functorial Data Migration*. functors.md:12-17 gives the four signatures: `a → Either Error a`, `DataId → Either Error Row`, `Row → Either Error ()`, `a → EventRef`.
- **Why it is wrong:** None of the four is a mapping between categories. An arrow of the schema category is a morphism, which the doc says itself one paragraph after the definition. In the Spivak formalism it cites, the schema is a finitely presented category, the *instance* is the functor (schema → Set), and constraints are equations in the presentation. The second sentence of line 16 is the accurate description and it contradicts the first.
- **Fix:** Rewrite docs/category-model.md:16 to define the term as DataCode uses it — "a named, transparent, first-class rule attached to a schema object, compiled to a DSL term" — and add one sentence saying the word is used more loosely than in Spivak's presentation, where the functor is the instance and constraints are equations. Keep the four kinds as they are.

### [minor] Presence and absence are called "the other two shapes of the same kind" while the presentation defined three lines earlier admits only equations

- **Where:** docs/category-model.md:134-137, docs/category-model.md:141, docs/category-model.md:40, docs/schema/functors.md:136-141, docs/distribution.md:442-457
- **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE
- **Evidence:** category-model.md:134-137 — "A schema is a **finitely presented category** where: Objects = tables … Morphisms = foreign keys … Equations = commutative diagram constraints (path equivalences)". category-model.md:141 — "**Presence** asserts that the set of rows reached by a composition is inhabited, and **absence** that it is empty — **neither is an equation** … They are admitted as the other two shapes of the same kind". category-model.md:40 — "The comma-category framing is what makes the last two well-posed rather than ad hoc".
- **Why it is wrong:** The presentation as defined at 134-137 has exactly three ingredients — objects, morphisms, equations — and line 141 concedes presence and absence are none of them, so "the other two shapes of the same kind" is not supported by the framing the section builds. The precise classification exists and buys the design something: a path equivalence is an equality-generating dependency, presence is a tuple-generating dependency, and absence is a denial constraint. The first two are monotone and survive append-only merge replication; a denial constraint does not — a `not $ …` assert satisfied at commit can be falsified by an insert to a different table in a different shard, which is exactly the failure OQ-027:144 and distribution.md:442-457 discovered per-case and patched with the `enforce always` restriction.
- **Fix:** In docs/category-model.md#path-equivalence-david-spivak-model replace "admitted as the other two shapes of the same kind" with the classification: "a path equivalence is an equality-generating dependency, presence a tuple-generating dependency, and absence a denial constraint. The first two are monotone and survive merge replication; the third is not, which is why distribution.md restricts a cross-shard absence assert's enforcement mode." Add one sentence to constraints.md#absence pointing at that consequence.
- **Verifier note:** Narrowed the candidate substantially: category-model.md:141 already concedes "neither is an equation", so the doc is not as overstated as claimed. What survives is the mismatch with the three-ingredient presentation at 134-137, and the fact that the monotonicity consequence is nowhere stated (grep for monotone/CALM/denial constraint finds nothing in this context).

### [minor] `Event a ≅ [(Time, a)]` "is the storage format" requires a total time order the design says it does not have, and no behavior combinators exist

- **Where:** docs/category-model.md:107, docs/category-model.md:110-114, docs/schema/types.md:139-141, docs/schema/types.md:294-296, docs/schema/railroad.md:171
- **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE
- **Evidence:** category-model.md:107 — "| Append-only, no in-place update, idempotent records | A row's history *is* `Event a ≅ [(Time, a)]`. **Not an analogy; it is the storage format.** |"; category-model.md:110 — "The two FRP primitives are therefore already present." Against queries.md:404-407 (per-server wall clocks with regression clamping, which is why the coordinating server must resolve one moment) and the branch/merge structure the transaction graph is built on. types.md:139-141 — "Two behaviors can be combined **pointwise** only if they share a domain", offered as rationale with no syntax for combining them; railroad.md:171 rejects a `Behavior` field in a `RecordLit`, and types.md:287-292 rejects it in `unique`, `indexed`, `order by`, and `where`.
- **Why it is wrong:** `Event a ≅ [(Time, a)]` needs `Time` to be a total order; the log is a branching DAG and its timestamps are per-server wall clocks. The accurate weaker claim is that a single row's version chain within one shard is an `Event a`. Separately, the FRP *types* are present but essentially all of FRP's content is the combinators, and none exist in the surface language — no `Functor`/`Applicative` over `Behavior`, no `stepper`/`accumB`, no `switcher`. The one genuine `Behavior`-to-`Event` operator is the `on <behavior condition> emit` form, which OQ-034 leaves unimplemented.
- **Fix:** In docs/category-model.md#denotative-time weaken the table row to "a row's version chain within one shard is an `Event a`; the graph as a whole is a branching DAG and is not." Add one sentence after line 110: "The design adopts the denotational discipline — time as a parameter, meaning independent of evaluation — rather than an FRP combinator library. `on <behavior> emit` is the only `Behavior`-to-`Event` operator, deliberately."

### [minor] category-model.md calls DataCode's rules "functors" while simultaneously identifying them as morphisms

- **Where:** docs/category-model.md:16, docs/category-model.md:29, docs/category-model.md:36, docs/category-model.md:134-139, docs/schema/functors.md:12-17
- **Evidence:** category-model.md:16: "A functor in DataCode is a structure-preserving mapping between categories. In practice, each functor is a Haskell function applied to a type or relationship that enforces a rule." category-model.md:29 describes foreign-key functors as things that "Encode the \"arrows\" of the schema category". category-model.md:134-136 states the Spivak model: "Objects = tables (or types); Morphisms = foreign keys and functional dependencies". functors.md:12-17 gives the four signatures — `a → Either Error a`, `DataId → Either Error Row`, `Row → Either Error ()`, `a → EventRef`.
- **Why it is wrong:** The two sentences at line 16 contradict each other, and line 29 contradicts line 36's own citation. In Spivak's functorial data migration a schema is a category **C**, foreign keys are *morphisms* of **C**, and the functors are the instance functor **C** → **Set** and the schema morphisms inducing Δ/Σ/Π. Each of the four signatures in functors.md is a morphism (in a Kleisli category, for the `Either`-valued ones), not a functor: none maps objects to objects and morphisms to morphisms. Naming them "functors" while citing Spivak misattributes the formalism, and the doc's own line 29 and line 135 say "arrows"/"morphisms".
- **Fix:** Keep "functor" as DataCode's product term but say so explicitly once: at category-model.md:16, replace the definition with "DataCode calls these *functors* by long-standing convention; categorically each is a morphism — an arrow of the schema category or of its Kleisli category over `Either Error`. The functor in Spivak's sense is the instance assignment **C** → **Set** that they constrain." Leave functors.md's operational table unchanged.

### [minor] "Functor" is used for things the cited formalism calls morphisms, and the document says so in the same paragraph

In practice, each functor is a Haskell function applied to a type or relationship that enforces a rule." category-model.md:29-30, on kind 2 — "Encode the \"arrows\" of the schema category". category-model.md:134-136 — "A schema is a **finitely presented category** where: Objects = tables … Morphisms = foreign keys".
- **Why it is wrong:** Under Spivak's formalism the schema is a category, an instance is a functor C → **Set**, and a data migration is induced by a functor between schemas; a foreign key is a *morphism*, and a validation predicate or an event trigger is neither a functor nor a morphism between the categories named. The document states the correct definition (morphisms = foreign keys) two sections after calling the same thing a functor kind. The naming is settled and pervasive, so the fix is a disclaimer rather than a rename.

## docs/schema/queries.md

28 findings — 0 blocker, 17 major, 10 minor, 1 nit.

### [major] queries.md and types.md document a relational `|` union operator that the grammar lacks and railroad.md explicitly declined to add

- **Where:** docs/schema/queries.md:460, docs/schema/queries.md:479-485, docs/schema/types.md:79-80, docs/schema/railroad.md:602-624, docs/schema/railroad.md:1019-1022, docs/open-questions.md:379
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/railroad.md
- **Evidence:** queries.md:460 key-propagation row: "| `\|` union | The source key **plus a discriminator**, which may not exist |". queries.md:481: "**Union** does not preserve a shared key…". types.md:79-80: "The `|` operator builds sum types. This is the same operator used for relational union — context (type-annotation position vs. query-expression position) disambiguates." But railroad.md:603-616 gives `Query ::= Source QueryClause*` with no union alternative; `|` occurs only in `TypeExpr` and `JoinSource`. railroad.md:1019-1022 records `union`/`except`/`intersect` as considered and **not** reserved, "admitting them would raise key-reconciliation questions the language does not otherwise have to answer."
- **Why it is wrong:** There is no query-expression position in which `|` means union, so types.md's disambiguation rule describes nothing, and queries.md answers the very key-reconciliation question railroad.md says was avoided by not having the operator. The only union in the language is the implicit one over rollup levels (aggregates.md:76-90), which is not written with `|`.
- **Fix:** Change the queries.md:460 row from `| \| union |` to `| the rollup union over chain levels |` and rewrite queries.md:479-485 to say the only union is the one a `retain` chain generates, discriminated by `grain`. Delete the second sentence of types.md:79-80 (`|` in query position is outer-join alternation, not union). Adjust the corresponding clause in the OQ-005 bullet at open-questions.md:379 so it does not imply a writable union operator.

### [major] The `ServiceAccount` example omits a mandatory reverse-join `as` and declares an auth view `LogData`, contradicting auth.md and OQ-015

- **Where:** docs/schema/queries.md:299, docs/schema/queries.md:307-309, docs/schema/queries.md:533-546, docs/auth.md:72, docs/auth.md:485-498, docs/open-questions.md:863-870, docs/schema/railroad.md:670-673
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/queries.md
- **Evidence:** queries.md:299: `ServiceAccount : LogData = User >< AccountKind { User.*, AccountKind.purpose } where kind is Service`. auth.md:486 declares `user :> User` inside `table system.auth.AccountKind : Configuration`, so `AccountKind` is joined against the reference direction; railroad.md:670-672 makes `as` "**mandatory when a source joined against the reference direction is named anywhere in the query**", and it is named twice. auth.md:72 declares `table system.auth.User : Configuration`; auth.md:492-493 and OQ-015 (open-questions.md:863-865) write the same binding with **no** trait override and call it writable. traits.md:104 tabulates `LogData` as "Server-local, prunable", and tables.md:129-130 exempts it from the candidate key that queries.md:545 requires for the write-through demonstrated at queries.md:533.
- **Why it is wrong:** Three defects in one line: the mandatory `as` is missing so the example does not compile; both sources carry `Configuration`, so nothing forces an override and `LogData` is the wrong one to pick for an identity view that must resolve on every server; and `LogData` removes the key requirement the same file's write-through rule depends on. The illustration also sits under "a derived table over `LogData` was never free to be `UserData`", which is about the opposite direction.
- **Fix:** Rewrite docs/schema/queries.md:299 to match auth.md and OQ-015: `system.auth.ServiceAccount = system.auth.User >< AccountKind as ak { User.*, ak.purpose } where ak.kind is Service`, with no trait override. Add the same `as ak` to docs/auth.md:492-493 and to the OQ-015 answer at open-questions.md:863-865. Replace the trait-override illustration at queries.md:296-309 with one whose override is meaningful in the stated direction.

### [major] Write-through says constant equalities supply insert values, but the only example's filter uses `is`, not `==`

- **Where:** docs/schema/queries.md:537-539, docs/schema/queries.md:299, docs/auth.md:493, docs/schema/railroad.md:511-512
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/queries.md
- **Evidence:** queries.md:537-539: "**A `where` filter is a check constraint on write, and its constant equalities supply values on insert.** … where the filter pins a field to a constant, that constant is written." The filter that supplied `kind` is `where kind is Service` (queries.md:299, auth.md:493). railroad.md:511-512: "Comparison is always `==`. Constructor matching (ignoring payload) is `is`; exact equality including payload is `==`."
- **Why it is wrong:** `is` is a constructor match, not an equality, so the stated rule does not cover its only example. The distinction is load-bearing: for a payload-carrying variant `x is Waived` determines no value to write, so `is` does not in general pin a field to a constant.
- **Fix:** Restate the rule in docs/schema/queries.md#writing-through-a-derived-table naming both operators and their limits: a `where` conjunct `field == <literal>` supplies that literal on insert; `field is <nullary variant>` supplies that variant; `field is <payload-carrying variant>` pins nothing and leaves the field required, which then fails admissibility condition 3.

### [major] Clause-order semantics are undefined, and the `ServiceAccount` example filters on a column its own projection drops

- **Where:** docs/schema/queries.md:16-26, docs/schema/queries.md:299, docs/auth.md:492-493, docs/schema/railroad.md:603-616
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/queries.md
- **Evidence:** railroad.md:603 `Query ::= Source QueryClause*` with no ordering constraint and no constraint bullet about order. queries.md:16-26 shows source → `where` → projection. But queries.md:299 and auth.md:492-493 write `User >< AccountKind { User.*, AccountKind.purpose } where kind is Service` — the projection keeps only `User.*` and `AccountKind.purpose`, so `kind` is not a column of the projected relation, yet the following `where` names it.
- **Why it is wrong:** Nothing states whether `QueryClause`s apply in written order (making this a reference to a dropped column) or are gathered into a canonical pipeline (in which case the canonical order must be given, because it changes what `{ … }` then `where` means and interacts with the outer-join filter-placement rule at queries.md:150-166). queries.md is the query-semantics home and does not answer it.
- **Fix:** Add a short "Clause order" subsection to docs/schema/queries.md after #filter-projection-alias stating the evaluation rule explicitly, and add a matching one-line constraint bullet under railroad.md:665-678. If the rule is left-to-right, move `where kind is Service` before the projection in queries.md:299 and auth.md:492-493; if clauses are canonically reordered, state the canonical order and how it interacts with the filter-before-guard rule.

### [major] The shifted self-join that replaces window functions cannot be written: `><` has no join predicate

- **Where:** docs/schema/queries.md:387-388, docs/schema/railroad.md:618, docs/schema/railroad.md:667-669, docs/schema/railroad.md:1023-1025, docs/schema/queries.md:127-129
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/queries.md
- **Evidence:** queries.md:387-388: "Comparing aggregates over time needs neither `diff` nor window functions. A rollup level is a real table and queries compose, so a shifted self-join states it directly." railroad.md:1023-1025 rejects `window`, `over`, and `partition` on that argument. railroad.md:618 `JoinClause ::= '><' JoinSource ( 'via' QName )? ( 'as' Ident )?` — no predicate slot — and railroad.md:667-669 restricts `via` to a declared `:>` field or a `Null`-derived type.
- **Why it is wrong:** A period-over-period comparison joins a rollup level to itself on `bucket_start == prev.bucket_start + 1 * grain`. No `:>` edge exists for that, so the only legal spelling is `RequestRollup >< RequestRollup as prev via Unrelated where …` — a full self cross product filtered afterwards, which queries.md:127-129 says is "expensive enough to be worth making unwritable". No worked example of the idiom appears anywhere in docs/. This is the sole stated justification for having no window functions.
- **Fix:** Add a worked period-over-period example to docs/schema/queries.md#diffing-two-transaction-points and give it a spelling: either extend `JoinClause` in railroad.md:618 with an explicit equi-join form (`'via' Expr` restricted to an equality over one column per side), or add a `shift`/`lag` operator over a `Grain`-keyed table and document it in queries.md. If neither is wanted, withdraw the claim at queries.md:387-388 and the parallel one at railroad.md:1023-1025 and open an OQ for window functions.

### [major] "Stored rows make the moment immaterial" is contradicted by delete-tombstone visibility in the same file

- **Where:** docs/schema/queries.md:409-410, docs/schema/queries.md:584-586, docs/storage.md:200-202
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Normative home:** docs/schema/queries.md
- **Evidence:** queries.md:409-410: "Stored rows make the moment immaterial, which is why this has not needed stating until now. Over a behavior it is part of what the result means." queries.md:584-586: "The row is absent from any query whose sample moment is at or after the delete, and present in any query pinned earlier with `at`."
- **Why it is wrong:** The sample moment is exactly what decides whether a tombstoned row is visible, so it is not immaterial for stored rows — it is the visibility rule. storage.md:200-202 already models a query as a (commit node, sample moment) pair, which is the shape queries.md should be using here.
- **Fix:** Delete docs/schema/queries.md:409-410 and replace with: "A query resolves to a pair — the commit node, which decides which row versions exist, and the sample moment, which decides how behaviors are evaluated. See [Historical queries](#historical-queries) for how `at` sets each." This also gives the `at` gap below a place to be answered.
